video.title: This AI Finds the Idea, Customers, and Does the Work

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Alex from Hyper Agent (built by Airtable), a platform for persistent, named AI agents that browse the web, spin up sub-agents and run on schedules ('live mode'). Demos include an agent that finds local businesses with great reviews but no or poor websites and builds them new sites, an always-on 'Signal' outbound sales agent that builds personalised landing pages per prospect, a pond-dredging lead database proof of concept, and a Facebook Marketplace scout. Chris then uses Hyper Agent to research boring $500k businesses, builds a laundromat opportunity map and saves it as a daily 'Deal Scout' agent. Key takeaway: treat agents as 24/7 employees with narrow permissions, and use them for lead generation, personalised outreach and agency delivery; the content is largely a product demo with promotional bias.

video.title: How I Work: $140K/Month App Developer

summary: Starter Story 'How I Work' profile of Jay, a former Amazon software engineer who built a meetup app for solo travellers, expats and nomads. He says it launched about 15 months earlier, makes about $140k a month, has 1.8 million users and over 100k meetups, and was bootstrapped as a solo founder. Most of the video covers his daily routine, working from cafes while travelling, and staying close to users (e.g. four months in Bangkok). Key takeaway: build something you care about, stay on the ground with your users, and treat regret as the bigger risk.

video.title: This Ridiculously Simple Business Makes Him $4M/Year (Can’t Fail)

summary: David Heacock interviews Ian Dolberg, founder of Dolcore, a New York City (Staten Island) security guard agency started in 2018 after military service and years working for large guard firms. Revenue went from $90k in year one to about $670k, then $1.3M, then nearly $4M in 2024, dipping to $3.3M last year as client funding was cut. Ian describes cold-calling sales, shotgun hiring, regulatory barriers, thin margins (~7%) and price-driven RFP losses. He also launched a marketing agency (Black Op Digital) for other guard companies. The host pushes him on value proposition, retention and systems. Key takeaway: a people-heavy, regulated, low-margin service that grew via founder-led outbound sales and niche compliance moats, but it is not agent-automatable.

ideas.problem: Businesses need legally licensed guards reliably present; a single in-house guard calling out leaves them unprotected or unable to open, and in-house forces carry insurance and licensing burdens.
ideas.offer: Licensed, military-led guards from a pool of about 200, with callout cover, 24/7 central monitoring of guards, supervisors, SOPs, training and paperwork for prevailing-wage contracts; plus bespoke tech such as a vibe-coded gate access control system.

pricing.notes: Race to the bottom on bid rates; minimum wage rises push prices up and clients shop around.

acquisition_channels.details: Founder cold-called facilities managers, property managers and security directors; sent a letter and packet/trifold beforehand announcing a call time, then called; weekly batches of 10 LinkedIn-sourced contacts. Now a hired salesperson trained in his method (outbound calls and emails).
Connected with property managers on LinkedIn, pulled emails into an Excel sheet and followed up.
Paid $50 to join the Metropolitan Cemetery Association to reach cemetery directors; Staten Island Chamber of Commerce, golf committee and event sponsorships.
In-house SEO team plus Google Ads; about $135k a year on marketing; aims to respond to quote requests within 15 minutes.
Friend introductions (bank client via Statland Security owner, Snug Harbor event); guards alert him when a site gets a new security director.
Invited to many RFPs; bid about $100M in RFPs this year and won none because of price; DCAS-certified school list gives grant-funded school work.
Event videos and a guard music video on website, YouTube and social, linked in proposals instead of stock photos.

acquisition.how: Inbound SEO and ads can be automated, but his proven method is human phone outreach to decision makers and RFPs; cold email to limited companies is legal in the UK but calls need TPS screening.

onboarding.how: Needs licensed guards recruited, vetted, trained and placed at physical sites; contracts and site walkthroughs are mostly human.

delivery.how: Physical guarding by licensed humans; agents could only help with scheduling, monitoring and reporting.

billing.how: Hourly invoicing and payroll (including prevailing-wage paperwork) can be largely software-driven.

support.how: Callouts, guard no-shows and client complaints need a human dispatcher in real time.

uk_applicability.notes: UK equivalent exists, with Security Industry Authority licensing for guards and approved contractor scheme, Working Time/minimum wage rules and thin margins; NYC-specific laws (Security Guard Act, FO4 fire guard, DCAS, prevailing wage) do not apply. The model works with changes but is labour-heavy.

Client funding cuts and new security directors causing contract loss
High insurance costs and liability, for example nightclub premiums after the Astroworld incident

Dependence on the founder for sales
Cannot win national accounts

video.title: The Amazon Program Almost Nobody Is Actually Doing (Full-Time)

summary: Nate describes earning commissions by filming short product review videos and placing them on Amazon product pages; the videos can earn without an outside audience. His approach favors making many simple videos of products already available over extensive research and editing, while using product access, brand campaigns, and cross-posting to expand the business. He also explains ways to find products, including filming at neighbors’ homes and requesting brand samples, and discusses reselling products and coaching. The central takeaway is to start publishing, learn through practice, and treat the income and Amazon placement as variable rather than guaranteed.

risks: Amazon placement is algorithmic, can change without notice, and is not guaranteed.
Videos and earnings can decay over time; Amazon provides limited data for diagnosing performance.
High volume can mean many videos earn nothing, while a smaller number may account for much of the income.
Rage bait may create engagement but can damage trust and reputation; claims about products should remain accurate.
The transcript says Amazon removed on-site related-sale credit in April, reducing the value of some negative reviews.
Do not film products inside stores such as Walmart or Target; Nate says this can get an account removed.
Unsolicited brand messages sent at scale could create UK PECR issues when recipients are individuals or sole traders; outreach should be limited to lawful recipients or consented channels.

tactics.name: Apply with an existing social account, then build engagement if rejected
steps: Try a public account you already have, such as Facebook, YouTube, Pinterest, or TikTok.
If rejected, choose a niche for a new TikTok account.
Follow a few niche accounts, like and comment on related posts, then post niche content consistently for about two weeks.
Use questions to invite comments; Nate also suggests rage bait, which may harm trust and should be used cautiously.

quote.text: If you've got a public Facebook page, you've got a big YouTube, you've got even a small YouTube.

tactics.name: Start with products already at hand
steps: Walk through your home and identify products, household hardware, furniture, books, clothing, tools, and used items that match Amazon listings.
Film an item you already own instead of spending the same time researching whether it is a perfect opportunity.
Use a visual search tool to match an item to a listing before filming; Nate says not to film first and match later.

tactics.name: Keep simple reviews quick and useful
steps: Use a phone or camera and talk through what the product is, what you like, what you dislike, and who it suits.
Show the item in use when practical; use a face-on-camera format when it helps, but film the product alone when that is clearer.
Skip editing out minor mistakes or the start button when the edit adds no useful information.
Use ChatGPT for talking points if a beginner needs help structuring a review.

quote.text: I just point my camera, I hold the product like with this mouse, I keep the mouse close to my face.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Test length and format against the likely shopper
steps: Nate's current videos average two to three minutes; he previously aimed for roughly 45 to 85 seconds.
Test making a video 30% to 50% longer to increase watch time, while recognizing that Amazon's placement algorithm changes.
Use vertical video when shoppers are more likely to be on phones, such as for fashion or children's products; use horizontal for desktop-oriented products.
Try additional formats on the same product, such as an unboxing, an update, or a second orientation.

quote.text: So for me, that's been make my videos maybe 30 to 50% longer than I normally would, and that seemed to be working well for me.

tactics.name: Make multiple useful angles for strong products
steps: For a product that merits more coverage, make separate videos for unboxing, setup, features, mistakes, comparison, and a later update.
Use measurements or real-life demonstrations when they answer a likely shopper question.
Keep the review honest, including problems with a product and who should avoid it.

quote.text: So you can kind of come at it from so many different angles. There's not like a one size fits all for these things.
quote.speaker: Nate

tactics.name: Use nearby households and real environments as product sources
steps: Ask neighbors or friends for permission to film products they already own.
Nate offered a $20 Starbucks gift card for an afternoon of access to a large Lego collection.
Offer to house-sit or return for another session if a household has more products than can be filmed in one visit.
Film products in their natural environment, such as a handwashing station at a market, but do not film products inside retail stores.

tactics.name: Prioritize products with campaign commissions and manageable competition
steps: Scan possible products and check influencer counts and Creator Connections campaign information.
When time is limited, prioritize products with a strong campaign rate and fewer competing influencers.
Treat selection filters such as 500 monthly units, zero influencers, or a 20% campaign rate as examples to test, not guaranteed predictors.

tactics.name: Ask brands for samples, but account for the work and competition
steps: Find relevant Creator Connections campaigns and send a clear request to the brand for a product to review.
Do not assume the campaign statement about samples means the brand will refuse; Nate says it may be boilerplate.
Track response rates and product handling time, and do not let free samples crowd out simpler products already available.
In the UK, screen the recipient type and ensure any electronic marketing outreach complies with PECR.

quote.text: So request anything you want, and about 10% are going to reach back to you and say, OK, great.

Treat YouTube as an incremental revenue stream unless you are intentionally producing content for YouTube viewers.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jay, founder of Violoop, a $399 (Kickstarter) on-device AI agent box that watches your screen via USB-C, builds a private memory graph, drafts replies and documents, and runs tasks while you're away. Jay demos invoice logging, an email-to-QuickBooks quotation workflow and ad performance tracking, claiming users save about two hours a day. They discuss using AI context to find a business, Marketplace arbitrage, cheap storefront tests and localising open-source AI tools for Asian markets. The episode is largely a product promotion.

video.title: Forget Snack Machines. This One Refills Itself

summary: Chris Koerner interviews CJ, a Fort Worth operator of four outdoor ice and water vending machines (Everest, Cooler Ice, Twice the Ice, and a large Ice House America-style unit) with no employees beyond one part-time maintenance tech. CJ explains how he got in via his pool-service business's ice spend, why buying distressed existing machines and locations beats building from scratch, how revenue-share vs flat-rent leases work, and the claimed ~90% gross margins. He also covers sale multiples of 2-3x annual profit, avoiding financing, and low-cost entry from $500-$1,000 for a used small machine. Key takeaway: location and buying out stressed single-machine owners are the main levers, but the business needs physical servicing.

ideas.business_model: Per-sale coin/cash/card vending of bagged ice and water; revenue share or flat lease with landlord.
ideas.customer: Tradespeople (pool, yard, electrical crews), contractors, boaters/weekenders, and general public needing cheap ice and water.
ideas.problem: Gas stations and grocers charge high prices for ice (about $4 for 7 lb at CVS/Walgreens); trades buy ice daily.

video.title: I Mixed GPT-6 Astra with Higgsfield - It’s INSANE

summary: George McConnell demonstrates a workflow inside ChatGPT (called 'GPT-6 Astra') using the Higgsfield plugin to produce a full ad campaign for a pink iPhone case: a 30-second video ad, a 16:9 cinematic ad, five static stills, a reusable named AI model ('Victoria'), UGC-style photos, and UGC talking videos with hook variations. Takeaway: product ad creative (video, stills, AI influencer UGC) can be produced from a product photo and prompts in minutes, and the creator's tip is to post 3-5 versions with different hooks on TikTok then move the winner to Instagram/Facebook. It is a tool demo with no revenue or business numbers, and it promotes the Higgsfield plugin via affiliate-style links.

Generation takes about 40 seconds to 5 minutes per asset. Character is defined by a detailed prompt, named, then reused by name. Outputs are also viewable in the Higgsfield library.

lessons.lesson: Name a reusable AI character and attach the product reference every time to keep identity and product consistent across assets.

For each machine he gives a rough price, product ideas and sometimes a customer angle, such as selling to wineries, flower shops, cafes, taquerias or bubble tea shops. lessons.lesson: Partnering with an adjacent business that wants an upsell (florists, funeral services) gives a ready referral channel.
Free or very cheap raw materials, such as waste bottles, give high margins on a custom product.
Branding a product with the customer's own logo turns commodities into B2B merchandise sales.

Machine-based physical production caps automation: delivery stays manual, so choose the model that best fits agent-run operations.
Treat single anecdotes like the $500k-a-year pillow maker as unverified; validate demand before buying equipment.

video.title: The Most Overlooked $81K/Month Business Anyone Can Start

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Parker Smith, a 25-year-old former DoorDash driver who built and sold a remote cleaning business, runs a holiday lighting business, and in 85 days grew Raleigh Water Pros, a whole-home water filtration installer, to $81k in August revenue with ~$500 setup. He advertises a $2,699 installed price via static Meta ads to undercut $6-8k in-home-sales competitors, pays independent plumbers ~$500 per install, and runs ~40% gross margin with ~$175 CAC. He details speed-to-lead texting, relentless follow-up, Indeed plumber hiring, inventory management and review collection. Key takeaway: find high-ticket trade services with inflated market rates, wedge on price, and sub out the labour.

ideas.name: Price-led whole-home water filtration with subcontracted plumbers (Raleigh Water Pros)
ideas.one_liner: Sell whole-home softener/carbon systems plus RO drinking water at a transparent $2,699 installed price via Facebook ads, undercutting $6-8k in-home-sales competitors, with independent plumbers doing installs.
ideas.business_model: Per-install project sales (~40% gross margin, ~$1,000 net target per job)
ideas.customer: Homeowners in Raleigh, NC (ads targeted 30-60 age in radius), often already quoted by Culligan/Kinetico/Leaf Home
ideas.problem: Big brands charge $6-8k via elaborate in-home sales; many are priced out
ideas.offer: Flagship 10x54 mixed-bed resin+carbon tank with RO drinking water, installed for $2,699 incl. tax; upsells (~$500)

pricing.notes: Price chosen as cheapest that still nets ~$1,000/job; raise once reputation allows. Average ticket ~$3,000-3,300 with upsells.

acquisition_channels.details: ~95% of customers from Facebook/Meta lead-form ads; static image of the unit with '$2,699 installed'; broad radius geo + age 30-60; $100-400/day spend; $30-40 per lead; ~$175 CAC.

quote.text: it was just a static image ad that was a photo of our unit and it said $26.99 installed and that was it
quote.speaker: Parker Smith

acquisition_channels.details: 52 five-star reviews in ~80 days; #1 for water filtration on east Raleigh.
Remaining ~5% from referrals and GBP.

ideas.delivery: Licensed independent plumbers (hired via sponsored Indeed post) install in ~4 hours for ~$400-650; inventory in a smart-lock storage unit with LTL freight; operations manager owns lead-to-install; GHL auto-texts new leads, humans call.
unit_economics_claims: $2,700 sale: ~$950 hardware, ~$100 misc, ~$500 plumber = ~40% gross margin
CAC ~$175; $30-40 per Meta lead
June ~$15k (5 installs), July ~$50k (16 jobs), August $81k (~25 jobs)
25% lead-to-close; ~35% of contacted
Ops manager $200 per closed job + base
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: First sale on day one of ads (June 8) with $41 of ad spend

acquisition.how: Meta ads can be run by agents with spend approval; lead-form leads in UK are opt-in so follow-up texts/calls to people who requested a quote are allowed, but closing still relies on human calls.

onboarding.how: Phone qualification and quotes by humans; automated intro text.

delivery.how: Physical installation by plumbers; inventory handling.

support.how: Plumber coordination and service issues human.

uk_applicability.notes: UK has hard-water regions (London/South East) and water softener market; needs WRAS-compliant installs and Gas Safe not required; prices in GBP; Meta ads work similarly. UK homes rarely have garages for tanks; softeners go under sinks.

risks: Inventory delays stalled installs
Plumber quality and dependency
Thin follow-up capacity as a one-man show
Rising CAC
Warranty/service obligations

video.title: He Built a $40k/Month Side Hustle Before Quitting His Job (Here's How)

summary: Phil built a UK e-commerce store selling campervan, caravan and motorhome accessories while keeping his digital marketing job, then left after the business sustained £40,000 in monthly revenue for six months. He started by researching high-ticket products, getting supplier approval and selling through dropshipping, using Google Shopping Ads for high-intent searches and later adding search-focused content. The business grew to a small team, with customer service and order follow-up outsourced and some best-selling stock held directly. His main caution is that this is active work, and revenue alone is a poor measure of success: profit, customer service and supplier reliability matter.

ideas.name: Campervan, caravan and motorhome accessories e-commerce
ideas.one_liner: An authorized online retailer sells specialist, high-ticket camping and vehicle accessories supplied by established brands.
ideas.business_model: Dropship retailer earning the difference between supplier cost and retail price; later, buy stock of proven products for improved margins, with own-brand products planned.
ideas.customer: People with an interest in campervans, caravans, RVs and motorhomes who need specialist products and may want help choosing or installing them.
ideas.problem: Customers need specialist products that may be hard to find locally, and may have questions about fit, sizing, installation, stock or delivery before making a high-value purchase.
ideas.offer: An online shop for products from authorized supplier brands, with product information, reviews where available, a contact number for questions and customer support. Suppliers initially ship orders directly to customers.

pricing.model: Product sales at retail price; the seller pays the supplier for each order and keeps the gross margin. Actual prices and supplier terms vary by brand and product.
pricing.notes: The transcript describes products retailing for $1,000 or more, but gives no complete price list. Phil says margins vary by supplier and product.

acquisition_channels.details: Phil used Google Shopping Ads to reach people searching for specific products. He divided the same products across upper-, middle- and bottom-funnel campaigns and used negative keywords to push broad or less-intent searches out of the bottom-funnel campaign.

quote.text: So you set up those three campaigns. You've got the same products being shown in all of them, need to be exactly the same.
quote.speaker: Phil

acquisition_channels.details: He later added informational articles, product comparisons, brand-versus-brand content and collection pages aimed at specific, lower-competition searches.

quote.text: I would say, honestly, one of if not the biggest lever that we've managed to pull in the last year or so is organic traffic.
quote.speaker: Phil

acquisition_channels.details: To recruit suppliers, Phil applied through dealer pages where available and called suppliers to speak with sales managers. These calls were supplier outreach, not the main customer-acquisition channel. In the UK, marketing calls must be screened against TPS/CTPS.

quote.text: So just fill those out if they have them, try and call them and speak to someone directly, speak to a sales manager and just explain a little bit about what you're looking to do and the value you can bring
quote.speaker: Phil

acquisition_channels.details: Phil says a phone number on the site helped customers get answers and that talking with early prospects helped win initial sales.

quote.text: I can't overemphasize how important it is to try and get people on the phone in the early days.
quote.speaker: Phil

ideas.delivery: The retailer lists supplier products on its site and takes orders. At the start, it held no stock: the supplier shipped each order. The founder initially answered product questions and handled some sales; later a small team handled most post-sale work. The business later used a 3PL for returned stock and began holding its best-selling products. Some products require installation by local companies.
unit_economics_claims: Phil says high-ticket products can leave $150 to a few thousand dollars of profit per sale, depending on product and supplier.
He reports gross margins of 15% to 40% across products, with lower percentages on some very high-ticket products.
He says bottom-funnel Google Shopping clicks may cost £1 to £5, so allowable acquisition cost depends on each product's margin.
He reports 1,200 to 1,500 orders and approximately 10 to 12 returns over 18 months.
He says holding stock may improve margins by 10% to 15% or more, but this requires choosing products with proven sales.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The host mentions $500 as a comparison for a hypothetical small ad test, not as Phil's actual startup spend.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. Phil describes his first sale, but gives no elapsed time from launch.

acquisition.how: Shopping campaigns and SEO can bring in inbound visitors after setup, and routine bidding or reporting can be assisted by software. Supplier applications and calls, early phone sales and campaign decisions still need human work. Any UK marketing calls require TPS/CTPS screening.

onboarding.how: An online checkout can collect orders and customer details, but supplier approval, product setup, brand guidelines and exceptions need human attention.

delivery.how: The supplier or 3PL handles fulfilment, but products still need physical packing and delivery; some installations also require local contractors.

billing.how: Online checkout and payment processing can run routinely. Supplier payment, refunds and unusual order issues may need a person.

support.how: A team can handle routine tracking and order questions, but product-fit, installation and high-value purchase questions often need a person who can check with suppliers.

uk_applicability.notes: Phil operates a UK store and explicitly discusses UK market conditions. The model works in the UK, subject to supplier availability, shipping arrangements, consumer returns obligations and compliant outbound marketing.

risks: The business is not passive: supplier recruitment, ad management, customer questions and issue resolution require ongoing work.
High-value purchases can generate detailed pre-sale questions, and a founder may need to learn product specifications or check answers with suppliers.
Dropshipping depends on suppliers' stock information and logistics; one supplier's installation company withdrew from multiple jobs, forcing a last-minute search for local installers.
Customers compare identical products across retailers, creating pressure to distinguish the offer through service, clear returns terms or other benefits.
Offering a longer returns window than the supplier creates exposure if a product is returned outside the supplier's own window.
Some brands sell directly to customers or restrict trademark bidding, which can limit the reseller's ability to compete.
Supplier outreach by UK cold calls must account for TPS/CTPS screening; unsolicited electronic marketing to individuals and sole traders requires consent under the rules provided for this task.

video.title: How I Built This $160K/Month Gym App

summary: Starter Story's Pat Walls interviews Mauro, a 22-23-year-old founder of Symmetry, a gym tracking app localised for Spain and Mexico that reports about $160k monthly revenue and about $3 million total after one year. Growth came from UGC rather than their YouTube audience or influencers: nearly 80,000 videos across 500+ accounts, almost a billion views, with nearly half of revenue paid to creators. The core of the interview is his product method: set ambitious quarterly OKRs, instrument every onboarding screen, use interviews for the 'why', start from problems, and A/B test everything for at least two weeks with guardrail metrics. A single commitment screen added 3% retention while redesigns of the home screen moved nothing. Key takeaway: localise into an underserved market and let experiments, not instinct, decide what to build.

video.title: I Just Sold a Niche Software Tool for $2.7 Million…Here’s How

summary: Spencer Haws of Niche Pursuits tells how he built and sold Link Whisper, a WordPress internal-linking plugin, for $2.7 million in January 2025. He covers three ways to find software ideas (scratch your own itch, find a gap in big players' features, interview customers), seven marketing strategies, and the broker-led sale process, which was slowed by an SBA loan, a bank switch and a slow buyer's attorney. Key takeaway: a niche plugin with an existing audience, a strong product and affiliate/marketplace distribution reached about $90k/month and an exit via Quiet Light.

summary: David Heacock (Boring Money) coaches Ron Butler, a 30-something master electrician who left an $83k job to start Top-Notch Electrical Services in Austin. Ron did $131k gross and $91k net in year one and $185k over the last 12 months, mostly remodel electrical work fed by nine general contractors he won through cold calls and in-person meetings, with ~70% margins. David's diagnosis: the pipeline is the bottleneck, so Ron should outsource delivery to 1099 crews, skip hiring a full-time electrician, and build a systematic contractor-acquisition process (master list, permit data, outreach) to go from 9 to 50 contractors and $1M revenue. They also question an out-of-state 'master on record' side income because of liability.

summary: Codie Sanchez explains a four-part sales framework: fix mindset (don't sell from your own wallet, sell from confidence not need), fix the message (current state, future state, bridge, with the buyer stating the gap and numbers), fix the proof (named, faced, specific testimonials plus anti-sales), and fix the avatar (find people already in pain, sell oxygen not dessert). She promotes her Boardroom community, an upcoming book and a HubSpot growth kit. Key takeaway: ask questions so the buyer sells themselves, price against the cost of the problem, and target buyers already feeling the pain.

Only then present your product as the bridge, restating their numbers

Target people already in pain with a budget
Score prospects as financially ready, reliable, right fit, energising
Ask whether your offer is oxygen (something breaks if no) or dessert

quote.text: You don't sell anyone anything. You find the people already predisposed to what the thing that you are selling.

tactics.name: Replace needy phrases with confident ones

Instead of handing off the work, ask 'Does option A or B work better for you?'
Instead of discounting, show the ROI or offer a more expensive option

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Nathan, a 31-year-old with a full-time auction job, who bought 10 used trailers from a retiring local operator in Lancaster, Pennsylvania for 35,000 USD and turned them into a contactless trailer rental business. After 15 months it grosses 5,500-7,500 USD a month with about 2,000-2,500 USD of overhead, taking him 2-5 hours a week. He explains the lockbox self-pickup system, pricing at ~1.5% of purchase price per day, deposits, insurance, maintenance and lead sources (Google 55%, Facebook 14%). Key takeaway: a low-tech rental asset with systemised booking can be nearly passive, and expansion via cloned small lots is the next step.

video.title: Why People Are Starting This Business Instead of Buying A Franchise

summary: The host compares buying a franchise with building an independent remote residential cleaning company, where independent cleaners do the physical work and the owner manages the operating systems. He argues that a franchise is most valuable when its brand creates demand, while home-service customers tend to choose highly rated providers who answer quickly and make booking easy. He describes his own window-cleaning experience, promotes Home Service Academy as a source of systems and coaching, and shares revenue claims for his businesses and a student. His central advice is to weigh franchise fees against the value of the brand and support, and to treat a first business as a way to learn transferable skills.

ideas.problem: Homes get dirty repeatedly, and customers want a reliable cleaner who answers the phone, shows up, does a good job, and makes booking easy.
ideas.offer: A local residential cleaning service. The company handles marketing, pricing, bookings, scheduling, customer service, recruiting, quality control, and finance; independent contractors perform the cleaning and bring their own equipment.

tools: Facebook ads (mentioned as a skill the host might have learned sooner)

acquisition.how: Agents could maintain local search listings, draft content, and manage inbound lead workflows, with a person checking ad decisions and handling exceptions. The transcript emphasizes reviews and answering calls.

onboarding.how: Agents could collect home details, match a customer to a cleaner, and schedule recurring visits, with human review for unusual requirements.

delivery.how: A cleaner must physically enter and clean each home. This part cannot be done by software agents.

billing.how: Recurring charges and payment reminders could be handled by software, with occasional human review of disputes and failed payments.

support.how: Agents could answer routine booking questions, but missed cleaners, quality issues, and customer complaints need human oversight.

uk_applicability.notes: Residential cleaning and local search apply in the UK, but the US independent-contractor model cannot simply be copied: UK employment status and tax treatment need to be checked.

risks: Physical cleaning still requires people and local quality control, so the business cannot run unattended.
The owner remains responsible for customer acquisition, recruiting, scheduling, service failures, and the finances.
Using independent contractors in the UK requires careful review of employment-status and tax rules.
The host gives no customer-level cleaning prices or operating-cost breakdown, so the claimed revenue and margin do not show the economics of a new operator.

video.title: Make Money With This New AI Agent That Works 24/7

summary: Chris Koerner tries the agentic AI tool he calls 'Grok Bot' for the first time and uses it to build a 'Morning Lock' product: a Mac menu bar app plus Chrome extension that locks Gmail and the Mail app outside set hours (e.g. 5-10am), with an accountability password held by a spouse. He had Claude write the prompt, then Grok Bot built, tested and fixed the app via Replit, GitHub and Stripe in about 31 minutes of recording. He says he plans to sell it as a SaaS in a part two, but no sales or revenue are shown. The takeaway is that agentic AI can produce a working, personally useful software product from one detailed prompt; whether it sells is untested.

video.title: Forget Traditional Car Detailing (This is So Much Better)

summary: UpFlip host Paul interviews Alan of Go Detail, who built a multi-million-dollar car detailing business from age 17 and now sells a licence/mentoring system (about 250 licensees). The video covers starting mobile detailing for under $500, a 'service partner' model with zero startup cost, upselling a $200 job to about $1,000, industrial ceramic coatings on heavy equipment, ad channels (Google Local Service Ads, radio), hiring a salesperson early, and a student (Miguel) who claims growth from $30k to $180-190k a month. Much of it promotes Alan's licensing programme, so figures are unverified claims.

video.title: Watch Me Build an App With AI and Make a Sale in 85 Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner builds and markets Only Waivers, a subscription app for creating digital liability waivers and collecting signatures for youth activities. He uses AI coding and advertising tools, runs paid and organic tests, and works through payment and product bugs on camera. He reports one paying customer, but says his advertising spend so far is much higher than the first year’s $13 subscription revenue. The main takeaway is to test demand while building, then use customer behavior and real checkout results to guide fixes and marketing.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; builds and markets the app on camera.

ideas.name: Only Waivers
ideas.one_liner: A self-service app for event organizers to create digital waivers and collect signatures from participants or their parents.
ideas.business_model: Annual subscription or one-off lifetime payment.
ideas.customer: Initially, Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints ward and stake leaders organizing youth activities; also considered gyms, trampoline parks, and tour operators. Parents or guardians sign as end users.
ideas.problem: Paper or PDF permission forms are cumbersome to distribute, print, sign, and collect. Forms can be lost, and organizers may let a child attend without a waiver rather than turn them away.
ideas.offer: An organizer creates an event, optionally uploads a waiver PDF to emulate, and generates a shareable signing link. Signers enter participant and medical information and sign on a phone without creating an account. The organizer can access signed copies in an admin account; the app can provide a generic waiver template.

pricing.notes: The prompt initially specified $13 per year and no free plan. Chris later selected $17 lifetime access, after briefly considering $15 or $20. The first reported external customer bought the yearly plan.

acquisition_channels.details: Created Meta/Facebook ads with an on-camera video aimed at LDS organizers. Started with broad US targeting, then narrowed delivery to Utah after seeing ads served across many states. Used a Meta pixel and UTM parameters to measure activity and compare ads.

quote.text: Make the daily budget 200 instead of 20 because I want results as soon as possible.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Posted questions about the waiver pain point in relevant Facebook groups, attached a screenshot of the waiver, and planned to explain the product in comments. Some posts went to moderator approval.

quote.text: posts that have a picture or a video of some sort always perform better. Always.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Posted a factual story in relevant Reddit communities, initially without a link, then planned to answer comments and add the product name or link if the community response supported it. One post was removed by moderators.

quote.text: the best way to promote on Reddit is to just write a true factual story about what you've done and why you did it and not link to it.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Added a resources page and an SEO-friendly blog about sending liability waivers, with the aim of attracting search traffic and being recommended by ChatGPT.
Planned referral links in confirmation emails and signed-waiver emails so organizers and signers could discover the product.

quote.text: Referral footer in every signed waiver email a lifetime value past year one.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The organizer creates an event and signing link in the web app. Participants or parents complete the form and sign on a phone; signed digital copies are stored for the organizer. The software sends transactional emails. Chris built and maintained the app himself with an AI coding tool, fixed bugs, and handled early customer support. No human service is required for each waiver, though organizers must choose appropriate waiver language and review the records.
unit_economics_claims: The first reported external customer paid for the $13 yearly plan.
Chris said he had spent around $100 on ads and had spent six hours building the app offline by the time of the sale.
He reported a $0.68 Stripe fee on the first external subscription payment.
He said a $200 daily advertising budget could produce roughly 1 to 200 landing page views per day, and estimated that about 15 sales per day would be needed to break even on ad spend.
ideas.startup_cost: Chris paid $12 for the domain. He did not state a full startup cost. He later described roughly $100 of ad spend and six hours of offline app-building work.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: A paying customer bought the yearly plan during the video. The transcript does not state the exact elapsed time from starting the build to that sale.

acquisition.how: Agents can help configure and optimize paid ads, write copy, and support SEO content. A person still needs to choose the audience and offer, make or approve creative, check results, and comply with platform and UK marketing rules.

onboarding.how: Organizers can self-serve event creation and payment, and signers do not need an account. Human review may still be needed when an organizer needs help choosing a template or setting up an event.

delivery.how: The app generates links, collects form data and signatures, and stores copies automatically. Organizers still need to decide whether the waiver suits their event and check that the data is complete.

billing.how: Stripe handles checkout and recurring yearly billing. The founder had to connect the live account and troubleshoot sandbox-mode and checkout issues.

support.how: A contact form can route messages, but early bugs, billing problems, and questions about waiver wording are likely to need founder attention.

uk_applicability.notes: The web app, paid advertising, search, and digital signatures can be used in the UK, but the waiver wording, consumer terms, privacy handling, and treatment of children's sensitive medical information need UK-specific review. The initial LDS positioning and US ad targeting also need adaptation.

risks: A digital signature and template do not by themselves establish that a waiver is suitable or enforceable for a particular organization or activity.
Medical details and children's data create privacy and security obligations; the transcript does not describe a compliance review.
The app initially launched with missing fields and encountered checkout, Stripe live-mode, and contact-form bugs.
A low annual price may not support costly paid acquisition. Chris explicitly reported spending more on ads than the first customer's annual payment.
Paid advertising aimed broadly at cheap clicks may produce traffic from poor-fit audiences; Chris changed targeting after seeing delivery across many states.
A narrow religious niche may limit the initial market, while expansion into gyms, tours, or other organizations may require different forms, branding, and sales processes.
Only one external customer is reported, so retention, repeat usage, referrals, and viable acquisition costs are unproven.
Using a church waiver form as a blueprint requires care; Chris noted that the source form was copyrighted and said not to ship a clone.

video.title: Build Real Revenue in Just 15 Minutes a Day (No Ads, No Audience)

summary: Nick Loper (Side Hustle Show host) interviews Kyle, founder of a partnership-matching platform (Spark), about a four-stage partnership framework: Discover, Verify, Launch, Amplify (DVLA). The idea is to borrow existing audiences and trust via partners rather than build an audience first. Examples are given for pressure washing (realtor referral at 20%), subscription ecommerce (box-insert swaps), and a content membership (mom-influencer affiliates), with a four-bullet outreach template and a 15-minute-a-day routine. Takeaway: lead with value, run a small time-boxed minimum viable partnership, measure, then scale. The guest sells a partnership platform, so the advice is partly promotional.

summary: David Heacock interviews Justin, who was fired from TGI Fridays and later from a commercial floor care firm, and now runs Midland Floor Care, a commercial floor care business in the DC area that did close to $450k last year. Justin started in residential cleaning with rented Home Depot equipment and bought leads, then moved into commercial work after asking a Massage Envy owner who did her floors. He grew through franchise referrals, and later through government contracts and bidding to prime contractors. The coaching half concludes his limiting factor is sales. David recommends hiring one proven salesperson from competitors or adjacent markets on a commission-heavy plan, building the sales financial model first, and incentivising contractors as partners.

He says AI can now help create content and jingles, while networking remains the main way to find clients. tactics.name: Use one-to-one networking to sell a local presence audit
steps: Attend local business networking meetings regularly.
Ask owners whether they want to grow; Mike says owners who already have all the business they need are not prospects.
Arrange one-to-one conversations with business owners.
Show a concrete issue in their online presence and explain how fixing it could lead to more business.

quote.text: The job of networking is doing one-to- ons with business owners and showing them that this is important
quote.speaker: Mike

tactics.name: Turn service knowledge into search-focused content
steps: List specific problems customers search for, rather than writing broad claims such as "we kill bugs."
Ask the operator to explain each problem aloud.
Record and transcribe the explanation, then publish it as a blog post and podcast episode.
Keep publishing regularly; Mike says a podcast should not be abandoned after only a few episodes.

quote.text: it's easier to record and transcribe than it is to write. It's a shorter distance from your brain to your tongue than it is from your brain to your hands.
quote.speaker: Mike

tactics.name: Build a conversion-focused local landing page
steps: Use a clear headline that names the customer's problem and promises a specific resolution.
Put the headline, short video, social proof and call to action near the top of the page.
Make it easy for a mobile visitor to tap to call or book.
Create specific landing pages for the problems named in ads.

quote.text: Headline, video, social proof, sales letter, and then everything else is if you want to or not.
quote.speaker: Mike

tactics.name: Use SER-term jingles in skippable local ads
steps: Choose a distinctive search phrase and pair it with a short positioning statement.
Put the phrase and positioning in the opening seconds of the jingle.
Keep the jingle around 15 seconds.
Run the ad in the target local market and let interested viewers continue while skip impressions still deliver the opening phrase.

quote.text: So, frontload it with something that will teach your local market or your worldwide market for that.

Add the jingle, publish the content and use a transcript as a blog post.

video.title: 20 Years Of Money Advice in 22 Minutes (How I Made Millions)

summary: Codie Sanchez shares career and business lessons from her first 40 years, drawn from finance (Goldman Sachs, Credit Suisse) and building her own companies. Themes include risk and family, being around winners in person, self-advocacy, negotiating on outcomes, promoting your work, keeping emotions out of work, moving fast, hiring A players and firing quickly, and rejecting work-life balance in the building phase. There is no specific business idea; the video promotes her book 'Owner Beyond' and a live launch event with a $1M giveaway.

summary: David Heacock, founder of air filter company Filterby, explains why he wants to spend his profits on a large farm and argues that agriculture's real wealth lies in land, water rights, processing, branding and distribution rather than the raw commodity. He gives examples (almond dynasties, bee pollination rental, cattle land owners, pecan orchards) and says he would pick land near Charlottesville, Virginia, of about 1,000 acres, spend the first years improving soil, water and infrastructure, then layer on diversified livestock, orchards and a direct-to-consumer brand. The key takeaway is a long-horizon, ownership-minded, asset-compounding mindset; it is a motivational pitch, not an operational playbook.

summary: Chris Koerner explains buying a 231-acre cattle ranch (Triple 8 Ranch) about 57 miles from downtown Dallas for millions, negotiating almost $400k off the list price using Claude to critique the appraisal and a 2% commission rebate from his wife acting as agent, financed 85% by a farm credit lender at about 6.7%. He covers agricultural tax exemptions, floodplain pricing, aquifers and the seller relationship. He then lists monetisation ideas for land: grass-fed beef shares (about 40% net margin, no ranch needed), a grazing lease, shop rent, hunting leases, a Texas farm pond database, a ranch YouTube channel, tiny homes, Hipcamp/RV/Airbnb stays, rent-to-own highway land for portable storage, and heavy equipment flipping and rental. The key takeaway is that land can be monetised many ways and many of the ideas don't require owning land.

summary: David Heacock interviews JT, a former software engineer from Ohio who built JC Print Farm, a 3D printing business that grew from a few basement printers to about 105 machines and five staff. Revenue was $50k in year one, $400k in year two and $400k year-to-date in 2026; about half comes from their own product catalogue (gaming grips, sculptures, custom busts) sold on Amazon, Etsy, eBay and Shopify, with B2B short runs and print-on-demand fulfilment making up the rest. JT targets ~50% margins on own products versus ~10% on print-on-demand. David's advice is to stop drifting toward low-margin fulfilment and instead systematise a creative pipeline of niche product designs (more shots on goal) seeded to TikTok Shop micro-influencers on commission. Also covers co-founder buyout agreements, S-corp salary/distributions and saving for optionality.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Rachel, who with her husband runs a restaurant specials-board ad business in Missoula and Knoxville: they give venues a free dry-erase sandwich board and sell six ad slots to local businesses at 600 USD a year each (3,600 USD per board, ~400 USD cost). They found hosts with copy-paste Instagram DMs and filled boards using guided owner referrals (12-20 names, ~6 closes). The real money is the upsell: about half of 63 advertisers bought reputation management (~400 USD/month), websites (1,000-6,000 USD) or AI receptionists via a GoHighLevel agency. video.title: Success is Hard Until You Understand This Formula

summary: Codie Sanchez explains her 'AOV to CAC' formula: judge a business by first-order average order value against full customer acquisition cost, rather than lifetime value, which she argues is usually miscalculated and leads to burning cash. She covers raising AOV through value-based pricing (10-20% of value created) and by adding tiers, subscriptions, upsells and referrals, using a plumber example and her own Boardroom ladder. She then covers lowering CAC with owned demand (organic, referrals, partnerships, email) versus rented paid ads, and gives her media business's return on content spend. The takeaway is to aim for a 3:1 AOV:CAC ratio and check it weekly.

tactics.name: AOV-to-CAC ratio check
steps: Use first-order AOV, not projected LTV
Compute CAC = all acquisition spend incl. ads, marketing and sales labour / net new customers

Recompute weekly because CAC creeps up ~5% at a time

summary: UpFlip host Paul visits Emily and Jeff of Lancaster Cupcake in Pennsylvania, a 15-year-old business that grew from home baking after a Ponzi-scheme loss and a $1,400 start to roughly $3.5M revenue. The video covers production (a $20k depositor, a $60k walk-in oven, up to 6,000 cupcakes a day), cupcake trucks, three retail sites, a full P&L showing about 40% claimed margin, and the Profit First cash-flow method. Marketing relies mainly on a 50,000-person email list and a loyalty program. A flavour-creation challenge fails comically. Key takeaway: a physical, labour-heavy product business with strong repeat-customer email marketing and disciplined cost control.

video.title: The REAL Reason I Quit YouTube (And Why I’m Back)

summary: Spencer Haws of Niche Pursuits explains why he stopped posting on YouTube for a year and why he is returning. His channel served as a funnel (brand, email list, podcast) to sell his software, Long Tail Pro and later Link Whisper, which he sold for $2.7M in January 2025 after six years. He no longer needs the money, bought an e-commerce business with his brother, and discloses a benign pituitary tumour that explained his low motivation. Key takeaway: content channels are distribution for a product; evergreen videos compound.

video.title: I Found the Perfect First Business for Introverts

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Ryan Schuetter, a 24-26 year old introverted Cincinnati ex-hospital project manager ($52k/yr) who now earns roughly $10-15k/month as an AI implementation consultant and educator. He started by having ~100-150 free, non-salesy video calls with people in his personal network and business groups, converting about 12 into paying clients (~$25k lifetime from the first 12). His offers are private AI coaching ($5-10k/month), month-long cohort groups ($1,000 per seat), and one-off implementation builds ($1k-$20k), organised around his DASA framework (Diagnose, Articulate, Systemize, AI). Key takeaway: relationship-led, value-first outreach plus education and free content can win clients without sales experience, though the model is human-led and network-dependent.

video.title: How a Mobile Espresso Bike Built a $3 Million Coffee Empire

summary: Vlad describes building a mobile coffee business in Vancouver, first selling drinks on regular routes and later serving private events and corporate activations. He explains how testing locations, building a returning local customer base, and using events led him to manufacture and sell coffee bikes to other operators. He says his CoffeeBike World model includes an owner community and optional add-on services, without franchise royalties or marketing fees. The interview’s main lesson is to test and execute rather than overplan, while the physical work, food regulations, and people-led sales limit how independently agents could run the operation.

video.title: 100% REMOTE Boring Businesses (That Almost Never Fail)

summary: Tim Richard explains a remote home-service model: attract customers online, show upfront prices and booking, then send the work to local subcontractors and share the revenue. He describes his own junk-removal business and gives seven service niches, recommending gutter cleaning as the one he would start now. The video also cites reported earnings for other operators and search-volume claims, without showing independent evidence for them. Its main practical advice is to target specific, low-competition services, make pricing easy to understand, and build recurring work where possible.

speakers.name: Tim Richard
speakers.description: Solo narrator and operator of a junk-removal business.

ideas.name: Remote junk removal
ideas.one_liner: Build a local junk-removal brand, book customers online, and send jobs to local subcontractors.
ideas.business_model: Per-job service revenue shared between the operator and subcontractors.
ideas.customer: People who need junk, furniture, appliances, or other unwanted items removed.
ideas.problem: Customers need a convenient way to find and book removal services.
ideas.offer: A local service brand with targeted service pages, upfront prices, and online booking; subcontractors perform the removal.

pricing.model: Upfront per-job pricing; exact prices not stated.
pricing.notes: The speaker says customers see a price and can book online, but gives no junk-removal prices.

acquisition_channels.details: Tim says he builds city and service pages for specific, lower-competition searches such as couch removal and appliance recycling.

quote.text: I build pages for each one of those in each city, and it's a lot easier to rank on Google when you have a very specific page for a very specific service
quote.speaker: Tim Richard

acquisition_channels.details: He describes a Google business listing as part of the local home-service brand model.

ideas.delivery: Local subcontractors perform the removal work; the operator finds customers and passes jobs to them.
unit_economics_claims: Tim says his version of the model has almost no overhead and owns only a laptop; he gives no dollar cost or margin.
The described model takes a cut of each job, but no split is stated.

acquisition.how: Service pages can attract inbound search traffic, but creating pages and earning rankings require ongoing human review.

onboarding.how: Customers can provide job details and book online; unusual jobs may still need human review.

delivery.how: Software can route jobs, but subcontractors must physically collect and remove items.

billing.how: The described website accepts online booking and payment, which can be handled by software with occasional checks.

support.how: Routine booking questions could be answered with software, but disputes, access issues, and job changes need human handling.

uk_applicability.notes: The local booking and subcontractor model can work in UK towns. Local search demand, waste-carrier rules, insurance, and consumer pricing need UK-specific handling.

risks: The operator depends on subcontractors to deliver the service reliably.
Local competition can make broad junk-removal searches difficult to rank for.
Waste handling, insurance, and service quality create operational and regulatory responsibilities.

video.title: Watch Me Clone a $200K/Month Business in 5 Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner walks through GoHighLevel's public SaaSpreneur awards page, which lists white-label resellers by customer tier (gold 100+, platinum 500+, diamond 1,000+). He estimates revenue by multiplying public pricing by tier customer counts, then reverse-engineers businesses selling to local service niches: event rentals (Event Hawk), med spas, gyms (PushPress) and dental (Dental Implant Machine). His toolkit is the pricing page, Wayback Machine, Meta Ads Library, BuiltWith and LinkedIn. He ends with a live demo of a missed-call-text-back setup for roofers in GoHighLevel. The key takeaway is to pick a boring local niche, copy proven ads and offers, and resell white-labelled software, but all figures are his napkin estimates and he earns affiliate commission from GoHighLevel.

video.title: I Tried to Make $10K in 10 Days With Costco Returns

summary: Chris Koerner flies in Shannon, an experienced liquidation reseller, to teach him to buy Costco customer-return pallets via the B-Stock auction platform and resell them on Facebook Marketplace. They bid on two lots (18 pallets of appliances at about $243/unit and a 12-unit patio/shed/gazebo lot at about $222/unit landed) and then test, photograph, list and sell the items. Chris aimed for $10K profit in 10 days but took 12.5 days; exact final totals are not stated in the transcript. Key lessons: buy at a very low per-unit cost, list the best items first for momentum, respond fast, and cut prices when listings get no hits. This is hands-on physical work, not hands-off.

acquisition.how: Listing creation can be AI-assisted (ChatGPT titles and copy), but Facebook Marketplace has no sanctioned API for posting, and photos and video must be taken physically.

uk_applicability.notes: UK has equivalents (B-Stock UK, Costco UK liquidation pallets, Facebook Marketplace, eBay, Gumtree), but the Costco returns lots on B-Stock are US-centred. UK Consumer Rights Act applies to sales of used goods by traders, and sellers who resell regularly are trading, so need HMRC registration; electrical goods need PAT or safety care. Garage space and UK-sized appliances differ from the US.

video.title: Why Gourmet Mushrooms Are the Most Profitable Small-Space Business

summary: Side Hustle Show host Nick Loper interviews Kyle of 10 Mile Mushrooms (Pennsylvania), who started growing gourmet mushrooms with a $300 investment after searching for a niche, small-space business. He sold at farmers markets, then added tinctures, dried mushrooms, grow blocks sold to other farms, restaurant wholesale, and courses (Pro Grow Club, Farm Launch). The main takeaways are the high margin of specialty mushrooms, the USDA beginning farmer loan used to buy a warehouse and 70 acres, grant funding, and agritourism Airbnbs. Much of the land-hack and grant material is US-specific, and the guest sells programs.

summary: UpFlip profiles Hunter, who started Mountain View Mushrooms in Northeast Pennsylvania at 17 from a grow kit. He demonstrates a cheap bucket-and-straw oyster grow, his home lab with HEPA hood and DIY pasteuriser and bagger, and a barn grow room he uses free in exchange for caring for animals. He sells about 75% retail at farmers markets and 25% wholesale to restaurants; 2025 revenue was 36,657 USD with 17,474 USD expenses (~48% net), heavily seasonal and up to ~10k/month at peak. Takeaway: low startup cost and high margins, but it is a labour-heavy, in-person physical business.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Braden, a former territory sales manager from central Arkansas who started an estate sale company in 2017 with almost no capital. He explains the 35% commission model, three-day markdowns, lead sources (EstateSales.net, overflow from established companies, realtor meetings) and a warehouse model that combined up to 30 small estates into $20-30k weekend sales, peaking at $30-40k gross per month. The estate sale business became a funnel for off-market real estate: about 60 houses since 2018 via wholesaling, flips and mid-term rentals on Furnish Finder. Key takeaway: a low-capital, unsexy service that gives first access to distressed sellers can feed a much more profitable business.

video.title: You Don’t Need to Start a Business, Buy One of These 10 Instead

summary: Johnny Robinson (Johnny & Sergio, Home Service Academy) ranks 10 business types to buy from F to S tier using one test: would the business survive if the owner walked away tomorrow? Ecommerce/FBA, founder-brand businesses and first-timer franchises rank worst; laundromats mid; lawn care, fence/deck, pest control, waste routes and HVAC/plumbing rank higher; small ageing-owner cleaning companies rank S tier. The key takeaway is to buy sticky recurring customer lists from owners with no exit plan, using seller financing, then add systems. The video ends in a pitch for his Home Service Academy coaching, so the ranking is promotional.

summary: Codie Sanchez explains how wealthy people use debt: borrowing against securities instead of selling, buying businesses with SBA loans and seller financing, mortgages, and credit cards for float. video.title: The $0 Side Hustle Anyone Can Start

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Trevin, an Amazon Influencer Program creator and co-founder of the tool Viral View, about filming short product review videos with a phone and uploading them to Amazon product pages for commission. They cover approval steps (public social profile, then three human-reviewed videos for onsite placement), the Creator Connections boosted commissions (10-50%) that drive most earnings, getting free products from brands, cross-posting to YouTube with deep links, and scaling by outsourcing. Earnings claims are large (GBP-equivalent $1-3K/month typical, $25-40K top) but are second-hand or from the guest who sells a tool in this space. Key takeaway: a near-zero-cost, volume-driven affiliate video model, but filming is a human task and results are self-reported.

video.title: He Built This Business in One Weekend for $40

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Spencer, who built a custom pet portrait business (transcribed as 'Printer Pet') over one weekend on Shopify for about $40, using print-on-demand fulfilment and commissioned artists in the Philippines. It launched in November 2019, took off with COVID pet adoption and Etsy, and hit just over $1M revenue in its first full year with over $800k in November-December alone; sales are highly seasonal and now declining. Chris advises fresh-creative Facebook ads (his Texas Snacks gets 10x ROAS at $500/day), testing whether customers actually prefer cheaper AI art, and live selling on Whatnot/TikTok Live. He also pitches Nano Banana side ideas: AI landscaping mock-up leads for landscapers and $1-per-photo AI virtual staging for listing agents. Transcript is Whisper (mis-heard names and numbers).

summary: UpFlip profiles Vicki Cakes, a pancake and waffle mix brand run by married couple Christian and Courtney, based on his mother-in-law Vicky's 45-year-old recipe. They started with $12.17 (a domain name and pre-order website), made $7,000 in year one, and claim about $1M revenue in 2025 with an 86% margin and roughly $3,400 of marketing spend, mostly via TikTok Shop (83% of revenue) and affiliates. video.title: This BORING Business Makes $3M/yr From My Laptop

summary: Tim Richard explains how his junk removal company became a nationwide remote business: customers book fixed-price item pickups (couches, TVs, appliances) online, and jobs are dispatched via Zenbooker to a database of 5,000+ local subcontractors, with ~50% margin per job. Growth came from unique city-by-item SEO pages, no paid ads; it now operates in 40+ cities and does well into seven figures. He says the model works for any service that can be priced upfront online. Takeaway: SEO plus fixed pricing plus subcontractor dispatch lets a local service run from a laptop.

video.title: She Makes $40K/Month with This Weird Hawaiian Dessert

summary: UpFlip visits Get Lost Shaved Ice in Virginia Beach, a Hawaiian shave ice shop opened in October 2023 by Stephanie and her husband Todd after a Hawaii honeymoon. They spent eight to nine months on recipe R&D, make about 10 dye-free syrups from scratch every Monday, sell $9.50-13.50 bowls with an estimated goods cost of cents per syrup portion, and run a food truck in summer (about 15% of revenue). 2025 revenue was $408.5k with a best month of about $95k, but after labour ($114k), rent ($50k+), $65k owner pay and other costs, net was about $23.5k; merch is claimed at about 20% of revenue at 50-60% margins. Lessons: the business is extremely seasonal and labour-heavy (3-4 staff in winter, 25 in summer), the buildout doubled from $60k, health department approval was hard, and a non-literal brand name enabled merch.

video.title: The Most Hands-Off $192K/M Business Anyone Can Copy

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Lou van der Vier, a former HR worker and SEO agency owner who fires his agency clients and builds local lead-generation websites (geography plus service, e.g. towing, carpet cleaning, concrete), which he rents to local contractors for a flat monthly fee. He claims 232 sites and $192.5K in a month, with a mostly VA-run operation and 2-3 hours a week. He walks through his niche-selection process live, and describes moving to revenue share, phantom equity (profit interest) deals, and buying a catering business with an SBA loan for tax reasons. Key takeaway: owning the ranking asset and renting the leads is more passive than agency work, but it all rests on Lou's own unverified claims, and Chris is also selling a done-for-you version of the service.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; also promotes a done-for-you lead gen site service.

speakers.name: Lou van der Vier
speakers.description: Rents lead-generation websites to local businesses; ex-HR worker, ex-SEO agency owner; also does revenue-share deals and business acquisitions.

ideas.name: Rank-and-rent local lead-gen websites
ideas.one_liner: Build exact-match geography+service SEO sites in low-competition local niches, rank them in Google organic and Maps, and rent the resulting calls/leads to a local business for a flat monthly fee.
ideas.business_model: Flat monthly rental of lead flow to one local contractor per site (billed by card on file); sometimes converted to revenue share.
ideas.customer: Owner-operated local service businesses (towing, tree service, pest control, carpet cleaning, concrete, landscaping design, HVAC, etc.) that already spend on ads and have a decision-maker reachable by phone.
ideas.problem: Small local businesses get inconsistent leads, have been burned by marketing agencies, and don't know how to rank in Google.
ideas.offer: Calls and quote requests routed to the business from a site ranking at the top of organic results and Maps, with call tracking, for a flat monthly fee.

pricing.model: Flat monthly fee per site, roughly based on lead volume and ticket size

price_points.label: Bigger flat-fee clients before moving to rev share
Range from weak to well-optimised sites per Lou

pricing.notes: Lou runs a few days of free leads to test a buyer, then charges a flat fee. Landscaping must generate about $8,000 jobs to be worth it. Dentists would be ideal but are hard to reach.

acquisition_channels.details: Customers for the rented leads come via Google organic and Maps rankings. Exact-match domains (geography+service.com), a thousand-plus words per page and a separate page per service, targeting keywords with 500+ searches. Small cities of 60K-400K, 'low competition'. Sites can rank without links.

quote.text: I have a thousand words on the item every time, for all services.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

acquisition_channels.details: Sets up Google Business profiles; the Woodside site was number one in Maps instantly because the name matched the keyword. Later GBPs are obtained via the contractor, which Chris calls a 'false competitor'. A GBP suspension tanked the towing site.

To find paying buyers, Lou (now a VA) phones owners already advertising on Google or Meta, offering leads for a cut. He says most reply 'yeah, cool'. Where the owner is behind a gatekeeper he sometimes walks in. Buyers are tested by secret-shopper calls.

quote.text: I'm literally just calling the person and saying, hey, I know you don't know me from Adam, but I've got customers that want this.
quote.speaker: Lou van der Vier

ideas.delivery: Sites are built in WordPress (Weebly originally), content drafted with AI (probably Claude per Lou) by VAs and human edited. Calls are tracked in CallRail, rank reports are sent by a VA, and the leads route straight to the business owner. Lou checks a weekly rank report and call report; most sites are left alone. Buyer outreach is done by a VA.
unit_economics_claims: 232 sites; $192.5K in the last month
Over 90% net profit margin (Chris's figure), 2-3 hours/week
First six sites replaced ~$9.5K/month income
Carpet cleaning site rented at $500/month for years at about $10/month cost
Costs ~ $50K/year of VAs plus hosting, CallRail and rank tracking
ideas.startup_cost: not stated (domain plus cheap shared hosting; Lou says site cost is about $10 a month or less)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: About 2-3 months for the first six sites to rank, then rent them out; the first site took about 2.5 months to rank organically.

acquisition.how: The SEO and Maps side is inbound and can be agent-driven. Finding and pitching buyers needs phone calls, vetting and secret-shopping; this needs a human or VA. In the UK, cold outreach to sole traders is restricted by PECR/TPS.

onboarding.how: Short call to agree the deal, routing set-up, a few days of free trial, and manual vetting of buyers (checking they follow up the same day, answer professionally).

delivery.how: Agents can research niches, draft pages and FAQs, and monitor rankings and calls; VAs now do these. Link building and GBP creation still need people.

billing.how: Stripe card on file with auto-pay, no invoicing.

support.how: Mostly passive; handled via monitoring of ranks and call volume plus the occasional buyer conversation or replacement.

uk_applicability.notes: Local SEO and renting leads work the same in the UK, but the examples are US cities. UK constraints: PECR/TPS on cold calling sole traders, Google's rules on fake or virtual Business Profiles, the need to disclose ranking of lead-gen brands, and smaller local markets. Buyers like Checkatrade or MyBuilder compete for the same job.

risks: Google Business Profile suspension can tank a site (happened with Woodside towing)
Niches with long contracts (elevators) or middlemen (jets) don't rent out
Finding serious buyers is hard; some prideful owners won't pay even with obvious ROI
Buyer may stop following up leads or lie about closes
Rankings can be lost to competitors or algorithm changes
Fake or duplicate Business Profiles may breach Google policy
All figures are self-reported

video.title: The Top Wealth Killer No One Talks About

summary: Codie Sanchez describes five personal-finance 'leaks' that drain bank accounts and businesses: payments over price, convenience spending, lifestyle creep, emotional spending, and invisible subscription spending. She gives a fix for each, including a three-number test (sticker price, total interest, opportunity cost), a 50/30/20 split of raises, an 'emotional receipt', and a recurring-charge 'friction audit'. The key takeaway is to plug the leaks and then redirect money into cash-flowing assets. No business idea is pitched.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Alex Kirby, a former pastor and landscaping founder who sold his marketing agency and launched Bridgeway Global Staffing, which places vetted Latin American remote workers with US blue-collar small businesses. He claims about $100k in sales in the first 100 days from roughly 27-30 placements, charging a one-time fee of about 28% of first-year salary (roughly $4,500-5,200) plus an optional $200/month membership. The playbook covers getting first clients via texts to friends and network, sourcing and vetting talent through job boards and video applications, and a lean stack of QuickBooks plus a Lovable-built portal. Key takeaway: AI makes building easy, but distribution and proactive outreach remain the hard part.

video.title: Steal These 5 "Wild" Business Ideas Making $1000/Day

summary: Nick and Chandler discuss five unusual businesses: cake gifting for sales teams, a mobile dog gym, an AI history video channel, cat products and premium matchmaking. Chandler adds pressure washing and AI implementation as side-hustle ideas, then describes how partnerships and AI tools support his publishing business. The conversation emphasizes high-value problems, recurring revenue, low SKU counts and finding customers through existing audiences. Most figures for the featured businesses are reported by the host from external sources; Chandler gives more first-hand detail about his own business and experiments.

video.title: The Laziest Service Business That Can Make $373/Day+ (From Home)

summary: Sergio (of Johnny & Sergio) pitches the 'remote cleaning business': a local home-cleaning company where the owner handles marketing, booking and scheduling while vetted independent cleaners do the work for about half the $300-350 job price. He claims a $150-175 spread per job, $373/day from 2-3 jobs, and cites two friends (the Nates) who grew to $60k/month in Wisconsin. He details recruiting cleaners from Facebook/Nextdoor, a secret 'test clean' to screen for poaching, a neighbour 'grand opening' post for first customers, and calling within 10 minutes to convert to recurring. The video ends promoting their paid 10K 90-day launch kit.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Caleb Panza, co-founder of Post for Me, a $10/month social-media posting API for developers launched after he and his co-founder Matt lost their jobs. With ~500 X followers, Caleb posted Stripe MRR milestones publicly, and built a support-driven content engine (human live chat, Linear, NotebookLM, AI articles) that got them recommended by Google and LLMs. They went from $500 MRR at five months to $5k at eight months and past $10k, but churn rose from 10% to over 17%, so they paused features to fix retention. summary: Chris Koerner and Brandon Doyle walk through five offline side hustles framed around making $10K in a year, month, week or day: temporary construction fence rental, portable mini-mini-golf (and cornhole golf) rentals/installs, inflatable outdoor movie rentals, buying local original art abroad to resell, and flipping a pallet of auction rugs. The fullest case is Brandon's teenage son, who bought 115 auction rugs for about $1,500 and sold about 80 for over $3,000 to fund a first car. video.title: How a Boring Podcast Got Millions of Downloads & Built a Media Empire

summary: Catherine describes building Nothing Much Happens from a part-time sleep podcast into a media business with advertising, memberships and books. Its growth came from solving a widespread problem, consistent high-quality publishing, listener referrals and an Apple feature; she says she spent nothing on marketing until much later. The business has added premium subscriptions, video, an app and audiobooks while keeping its core stories human-written and narrated. The main lesson for an agent-led founder is that this model can automate subscriptions and distribution, but the creative product and listener trust still depend heavily on people.
