ideas.name: Nothing Much Happens sleep podcast and media business
ideas.one_liner: Publish human-written, narrated bedtime stories that help listeners relax and fall asleep, then earn from advertising and sponsorships.
ideas.business_model: Free podcast funded by advertising and sponsorships. The broader media business also has paid subscriptions and books, covered separately below.
ideas.customer: People who struggle to sleep and listeners seeking calming companionship, including people experiencing anxiety, grief or PTSD.
ideas.problem: Listeners need gentle, trustworthy audio that can help them settle down without jarring interruptions.
ideas.offer: Regularly released, researched and narrated bedtime stories built around calm pacing, sensory detail and familiar settings.

pricing.model: Free to listeners; advertising and sponsorship revenue. Ad rates not stated.
pricing.notes: Catherine says ads began around 2020. She restricted placements to pre-roll and the end of the introduction, with no interruptions after she had tucked listeners in.

acquisition_channels.details: Catherine says listeners recommended the show to others after it helped them sleep.

quote.text: Because if sleep is something you struggle with and you sort that out, that is a life changer. You're going to tell people about that.
quote.speaker: Catherine

acquisition_channels.details: She told friends on Facebook about the podcast.

quote.text: I just told people about it at my yoga studio, like told my friends on Facebook, but it started to gather kind of an organic momentum just from people telling people.
quote.speaker: Catherine

acquisition_channels.details: She told people at her yoga studio; Apple featured the show on its New and Noteworthy platform.

quote.text: And then Apple featured us on the new and noteworthy platform. And it just kept growing and growing.
quote.speaker: Catherine

acquisition_channels.details: The show also developed a YouTube audience, initially by posting audio with a logo and later with animated artwork.

quote.text: He's like, do you want to have a YouTube channel? And I was like, oh sure. And so he just stuck the label or the logo on the audio
quote.speaker: Catherine

ideas.delivery: Catherine researches, writes and records stories. Her engineer Bob fixes audio and helped set up the YouTube channel. A small boutique ad network sells advertising. Audio is distributed through podcast platforms; animated artwork is used for video versions.
unit_economics_claims: Catherine says the show reached 10 million downloads about a year after launch.
She says the show began earning money from ads around 2020.
She says she spent no money on marketing until the year before the interview.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; Catherine says she bought a microphone from Amazon, but gives no price.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Catherine says the show began making money in 2020; exact time from launch is not stated.

acquisition.how: Publishing, metadata and promotion can be scheduled or supported by agents, but discovery in this account relied on listener referrals, platform featuring and a distinctive human voice.

onboarding.how: Podcast platforms handle follows and playback. Creating a welcoming introduction and establishing listener trust still requires human editorial judgment.

delivery.how: The core work is human research, writing, performance and audio review. A text-to-speech agent could read stories, but would not reproduce the described voice, pacing and care without substantial human input.

billing.how: Ad sales were handled by networks and digital advertising can be administered through platforms; human review is still needed for suitable advertisers and placement.

support.how: Agents could handle routine questions, but listener messages can involve sensitive situations where a human response and careful moderation matter.

uk_applicability.notes: A sleep-story podcast and its inbound discovery channels work in the UK. Ad rules, platform terms and any health-related claims would need to fit UK requirements.

risks: The host describes podcasting as a difficult channel for building an audience, and the show initially grew slowly.
Restricting ad placements gives listeners a better experience but reduces available ad inventory and can make the show harder for networks to sell.
The audience's trust is tied to the sensitive moment of falling asleep; intrusive or unsuitable ads could damage that trust.
Catherine says other people steal her content. Platform dependence and imitation are additional risks.
The product depends on a steady supply of high-quality stories and on Catherine's continued ability to write and record.

ideas.business_model: Not stated; video distribution and any ad revenue were not discussed.
ideas.customer: Listeners who prefer watching calming video content or use video platforms to fall asleep.
ideas.problem: Some people already use screens at bedtime and want visual content designed to be less stimulating.
ideas.offer: The audio stories paired with gently animated illustrations that dim to black by the end.

acquisition_channels.details: The channel started with audio and a logo, then added animated artwork. The newer videos are also available on Spotify.

quote.text: So now just a little while ago, we launched our video version. And we have quite a bit of artwork that was created by the artist Laley Pivair
quote.speaker: Catherine

ideas.delivery: Catherine's audio is paired with artwork by illustrator Laley Pivair, who gently animates the illustrations. The videos are distributed on YouTube and Spotify.
unit_economics_claims: Catherine says the YouTube channel had about 20,000 subscribers before the team focused on improving its videos.

acquisition.how: Platforms can recommend videos and publishing can be scheduled, but strong discovery still depends on the show's audience and artwork.

onboarding.how: Platforms handle subscriptions and playback automatically; video design still needs to set a calming expectation.

delivery.how: Video hosting and playback are automatic, but people write, narrate, illustrate and animate the content.

billing.how: Platform monetization could be automated if used, but no revenue mechanism was stated.

support.how: Platforms can handle basic account functions; audience interaction and content questions still need moderation and human judgment.

uk_applicability.notes: YouTube and Spotify distribution can reach UK audiences, and animated sleep stories are not tied to a US-only market.

risks: The transcript gives no figures for video production costs or revenue.
A screen may be counterproductive for some people trying to sleep, even though the videos dim to black.
The format depends on animation and artwork, adding production work beyond audio.

quotes.text: And it is designed, it gets dimmer and dimmer and dimmer as you watch it. And by each time it is time to say sweet dreams, it is off to black.
quotes.speaker: Catherine

ideas.name: On the Street Where You Live audiobook
ideas.one_liner: Release a longer village-set story collection as an audiobook performed by Catherine and professional voice actors.
ideas.business_model: Audiobook sales through audiobook platforms; price, royalty and publishing terms not stated.
ideas.customer: Existing listeners and audiobook buyers who want longer stories about the village and its community.
ideas.problem: Listeners want more immersive stories and a new format with multiple voices.
ideas.offer: A book set over three days in the village, performed by Catherine and eight voice actors.

pricing.model: Audiobook pre-orders and sales through audiobook services.
pricing.notes: Price and royalty terms are not stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Catherine says the audiobook is available for pre-order wherever listeners buy audiobooks; the show also directs listeners to the Nothing Much Happens website.

quote.text: It's just a lovely bit of healing fiction and it comes out on July 28th and it is available for pre-order right now any place you listen to audio books.
quote.speaker: Catherine

ideas.delivery: Catherine and eight professional voice actors perform the audiobook. It is sold through audiobook platforms; specific services are not named.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; the audiobook was available for pre-order before its stated July 28 release.

acquisition.how: Existing listeners can be reached through the show's channels and platforms can surface the title. No specific campaign results are stated.

onboarding.how: Audiobook platforms handle purchases, downloads and playback.

delivery.how: Platforms deliver the finished audio automatically, but recording, acting and production require people.

billing.how: Retail platforms process customer payments; publisher and author royalty arrangements are not described.

support.how: Retailers can handle routine purchase issues, while content and author questions may need human responses.

uk_applicability.notes: Audiobook platforms can sell to UK listeners. Platform availability and publishing terms may vary, but the format is broadly applicable.

risks: No audiobook price, production cost, royalty rate or sales results are provided.
The production relies on multiple voice actors and therefore has more coordination than a single-narrator show.

tactics.name: Start with a real problem and a founder advantage
steps: Identify a problem you understand from repeated direct contact with customers.
Use experience from an existing job or business to shape a solution; Catherine drew on her yoga teaching and her own ability to sleep.
Test the solution as a small podcast instead of waiting for a book deal or a large launch.

quote.text: I just thought there's a problem. I know how to fix it. How can I help fix it? That was really the extent of my focus at the time.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Publish reliably and improve the product before chasing promotion
steps: Choose a release schedule you can keep.
Make the content quality and listener experience the main early focus.
Build a repeatable production calendar and publish when promised.

quote.text: That was really focused on just having the show publish when I said it was going to publish regularly and reliably and developing the content in a way that I felt like was going to be the highest quality it could be.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Let a meaningful result create referrals
steps: Solve a problem in a way customers can describe to someone else.
Tell people in the communities you already serve and let satisfied users recommend the product.
Use listener comments and customer feedback to see which results prompt sharing.

quote.text: Because if sleep is something you struggle with and you sort that out, that is a life changer. You're going to tell people about that.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Ask your network for a specific introduction
steps: Tell a trusted network what help you need.
Ask directly whether someone knows the right person.
Use the introduction to reach a qualified agent or partner.

quote.text: I reached out to the network I was with at the time. I said, do you know anybody? I'm never afraid to just ask for help
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Use proof of audience to open publishing doors
steps: Build a measurable audience around the core idea.
Work with a literary agent to turn the idea into a proposal.
Use evidence of demand when approaching publishers.

quote.text: I don't think I would have had that response if I didn't have 10 million downloads. That's what opened the doors for me.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Set ad placement rules around the product promise
steps: Decide which ad placements preserve the core experience before agreeing to a network deal.
Allow ads only before the sleep story or near the end of the introduction.
Do not interrupt after the listener has been tucked in.

quote.text: And it really shortened the list of advertisers for us. If we were with Stitcher and I heart at different times, and because we weren't always the lowest hanging fruit
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Choose an ad partner that understands the audience
steps: Compare ad networks based on how much effort they put into selling the show and whether their advertisers fit.
Explain why listeners are attentive even though they may be falling asleep.
Move to a smaller specialist network if it provides more focused sales support.

quote.text: So we then moved to just in the last two years to a much smaller kind of boutique network, and it has been such a good choice for us.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Hand off specialist work when it is outside your skill set
steps: Identify work that is distracting from making the product or that you do not know how to negotiate.
Use an agent, manager or specialist partner for that work.
Keep your own time focused on the product you are best at creating.

quote.text: I just knew enough to know I would not be successful in trying to negotiate those things myself. Luckily, by the time we moved a little bit forward in time, I had a manager, I had an agent
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Make premium access easy in the listener's existing player
steps: Offer ad-free and bonus content through a listener's familiar podcast player where possible.
Support both Apple and Android listeners through suitable routes.
Keep the free show available so a paid offer does not block existing listeners.

quote.text: For a lot of people, nothing changed, except for the logo was a little different and they didn't hear ads. And that's the level of experience I wanted people to have.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Present membership as optional support, not an apology
steps: Explain what paid members receive and that the free version remains available.
Frame the annual price as a small daily amount if that is accurate.
Ask confidently for payment instead of apologizing for charging for the work.

quote.text: Even though I understood that I deserved to be paid for the work I did, I still think I came at it from this place of I'm so sorry that I have to do this.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Keep a listener-friendly free experience
steps: Leave a meaningful free offering in place for listeners who do not want to subscribe.
Keep ads in a format and tone suited to the content.
Avoid changing the free experience in ways that undermine trust as paid membership grows.

quote.text: And even now, we don't have programmatic ads on the first eight episodes. So you're only ever gonna hear my voice and I deliver ads in this tone of voice.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Build a story idea bank and revisit established storylines
steps: Record small moments that could become stories in a running notes list.
Return to characters and settings listeners already know.
Batch related writing into focused production periods.

quote.text: So I have a running list in my notes app that is probably 100 points long and I add to it constantly of ideas for stories.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Use a repeatable calming story structure
steps: Open with a naturally calming activity.
Add sensory details to make the listener feel present in the scene.
Use familiar or nostalgic situations and past-tense framing to reassure anxious listeners that events have already ended safely.
Leave characters unnamed so listeners can imagine themselves in the story.

quote.text: I also do stuff very deliberately, none of my characters have names. Because I want you to sort of feel like the character, you could be the innkeeper, you could be the baker
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Batch production ahead of release
steps: Write a month ahead using a strict calendar.
Group writing by show, then edit and record the batch.
Keep a schedule that matches the creator's energy and creative workflow.

quote.text: I write a month ahead and I have like a really strict calendar that I stick to.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Meet customers in the format they already use
steps: Offer the core content in audio, book and video formats when customer behavior supports them.
Design each format for its context, such as dimming video for bedtime.
Use the app concept to add playback features that standard podcast feeds cannot provide.

quote.text: My goal is always like, I'm gonna meet you where you are. If you've got your phone in your hand, I'm gonna meet you there. You read books, I'm gonna meet you there.
quote.speaker: Catherine

tactics.name: Do not wait to feel ready
steps: Make a decision to begin with a small experiment.
Learn from actual customers instead of waiting for confidence or perfect preparation.

quote.text: Stop waiting to feel ready. Ready isn't a feeling, it's a choice.
quote.speaker: Catherine

evidence_quality.rationale: The guest describes her own business and gives specific operating details, audience figures, membership renewal claims and production routines. Most financial figures are not independently verified, and the transcript is local Whisper output with several likely transcription errors.

summary: Tim Richard lists 10 low-cost local service businesses that can be started over a weekend: dog poop scooping, fence staining, photo organizing, garage cleaning, senior companion care, graffiti removal, cardboard recycling pickup, gutter cleaning, mattress and couch cleaning, and parking lot cleaning. Most examples are second-hand anecdotes with large income claims. The main marketing tactic is a personalised flyer with the owner's face and a written price for that specific property, plus local Facebook community posts. The video also promotes the host's paid 'idea book' database.

video.title: He Makes $1M a Year Selling Fish From His Backyard

summary: UpFlip visits Ty at Smoking Chimneys (as transcribed), a revitalised 1930s federal trout hatchery on four acres in Newcastle, southwest Virginia, fed by a 3,000-gallon-a-minute limestone spring. With zero fish experience, Ty spent a year cleaning the site, a year learning to raise trout and a year getting state processing approval, burned through $60k of savings and worked at a grocery store before reaching $120k in sales; the farm now does $1.1M revenue with about $218k (19.8%) net margin, selling 85% fresh to Michelin-star and high-end restaurants and 15% frozen/smoked to co-ops, grocers and direct-to-consumer boxes. Growth came with no debt and no ads, using organic reels, chef referrals and in-person cooler drops. The key lesson was raising price from $11.50/lb (below a $15/lb cost) to $18/lb, which saved the business.

video.title: 5 Ways to Make Money From an AI the Government Fears

summary: Chris Koerner says Anthropic's Fable 5 model was shut off worldwide three days after launch, after a US Commerce Department export-control letter. He claims its main strength is long-running autonomous work. He pitches five businesses to prepare now using weaker models: legacy code migration, overnight bookkeeping cleanup, an AI-staffed productized design studio, hyper-personalised email, and self-running website portfolios. Each is said to mirror an existing human-run business. The ideas are speculative and unvalidated, and the Fable claims are unverified. The takeaway is to build the niche, offer and landing page now with current models and not depend on a single AI tool.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Don, who runs a family fresh-squeezed lemonade business at the Frisco and Dallas farmers markets in Texas. It made about $250k last year over about 8 months, selling 32oz cups at $7 that cost about $1.25 to make. Don explains the recipe, equipment (about $1,500 to start), warehouse prep, staffing with his kids, a $300 booth fee, and expansion into $1,000-3,000 caterings, $500 cart rentals via Facebook Marketplace, venue concessions and a $19k frozen-banana trade-show job. summary: Side Hustle Nation host Nick Loper interviews Steve (App Masters, 17 years in app marketing, now acquiring and building vibe-coded apps). Steve's playbook: find keywords people search in the App Store (ASO), unbundle a feature from big apps, build a one-feature app named after the keyword, use a hard paywall with copied competitor pricing, and optionally run a lifetime-deal growth hack or Apple Search Ads. He claims apps earning from about $200/month to $35k MRR, and says roughly 40% of apps he launches make money. Key takeaway: distribution (ASO) matters more than features.

They are stainless steel litter boxes, hojicha latte, satin sheets, rice water shampoo, key fob covers, beef protein powder, men's crossbody bags, non-tarnish jewelry and floor couches. video.title: The Most Profitable Side Hustle No One Is Doing Yet

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Derek, who turned a $250-300 Amazon inflatable movie screen bought as a Christmas gift into Backyard Movie Theater in North Dallas. After a windy first HOA booking flopped, he bought a 20 ft commercial screen from Alibaba (~$3,500 plus ~$1,000 shipping), plus a $1,100 projector and two $1,500 JBL speakers, and sells packages from $375 to $1,500. He also designed a custom indoor air-conditioned inflatable theater (about $3,500 all-in, $1,700 per booking) because Texas summer movies can't start before 9:30pm, and added a $20k LED dance floor rented at $3,000. He claims $10k of bookings in one week, about $40k last year and $90-100k expected this year at 70-80% margins, mostly from Facebook Marketplace and referrals.

video.title: The Laziest AI Side Hustle Anyone Can Start Right Now

summary: Chris Koerner pitches a low-effort AI side hustle: cloning a realtor's voice with Fish Audio S2 Pro and generating pre-written voicemails in the languages of multilingual buyers, sold for about $200-500 a month. He demos the workflow (clone voice from a 17-second sample, draft scripts with an LLM, translate, generate audio, save to Google Drive) and claims it costs cents per message. He then lists adjacent ideas (audiobook narration, YouTube dubbing, local-business voiceover, other multilingual professions) and a day-by-day plan to land the first clients. Key takeaway: cheap voice-cloning tools let a solo operator sell a productised service, but the claims are hypothetical and the video promotes an affiliate-style code for Fish Audio.

ideas.offer: Clone the realtor's voice from a 30-60 second clip (or existing social video), then deliver a library of pre-recorded translated voicemails (new listing, price drop, showing confirmation, missed appointment, etc.) in the same voice.

pricing.notes: Suggests a one-time free or cheap package first to get a foot in the door, then upsell AI services.

acquisition.how: Friend outreach, lunches and visiting offices are human. Cold outreach to individual realtors (often sole traders) by SMS/DM/email is restricted under UK PECR; only inbound or limited-company email is feasible by software.

onboarding.how: Agent collects a voice clip or scrapes public video; consent and voice-rights capture can be a form flow, with human checks on consent.

delivery.how: LLM script writing, translation and TTS are scriptable via API, though the demo uses the UI one message at a time and a native speaker should check translations.

billing.how: Standard subscription billing via Stripe or similar.

support.how: Revision requests, re-recordings and translation complaints can be handled by an agent with human review.

uk_applicability.notes: Technology works the same, but the demand rests on US demographics and a US-style voicemail-driven realtor workflow. UK agents mostly use email and WhatsApp, and sending voicemails or automated marketing calls to leads is regulated by PECR and UK GDPR, and voice cloning needs documented consent. A UK version would target London and other multilingual markets and possibly other languages.

Voicemails sound accented; translation quality is unverified without native speakers.
Marketing voicemails and calls to leads are regulated (PECR/TCPA-type rules).
Clients may do it themselves once they learn the tool.
Dependence on one vendor (Fish Audio) pricing and terms.

video.title: He Made $60K His First Month With This Boring Business

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Mike from Iowa City, a tile installer who launched a garage-floor concrete coatings business (flake floors using polyurea base and polyaspartic top coat) around February-March 2026 with his brother and two experienced partners. He claims $60K revenue in April and $69K in May with over 50% profit, driven almost entirely by Meta ads, instant phone follow-up, upfront $8/sq ft pricing and a 10% deposit. Key takeaways: blue-collar service bars are low (answer the phone, show up, be transparent on price), AI (Claude) writes all ad copy and advises on ad budgets, and startup cost can be roughly $15-25K or under $1K by renting a grinder.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office

speakers.name: Mike
speakers.description: Tile contractor from Iowa City who runs Old Cap Coatings (concrete coatings) with partners; one of four partners

ideas.name: Garage floor flake coatings (Old Cap Coatings)
ideas.one_liner: Grind, coat and flake residential garage floors with polyurea base and polyaspartic top coat at $8/sq ft, one-day jobs, sold via Meta lead ads.
ideas.business_model: Per-job price per square foot with 10% non-refundable deposit; balance paid after the job.
ideas.customer: Mostly homeowners aged 50+, typically male, with 2-4 car garages; also some interior, patio, pool deck and commercial (a church, a warehouse).
ideas.problem: Bare or pitted concrete garage floors look bad and stain; owners want a decorative, easy-clean, durable finish.
ideas.offer: Decorative flake garage floor (grind, polyurea base coat, broadcast flake, polyaspartic top coat) installed in one day by a two-person crew, with optional move-your-stuff add-on.

pricing.model: Flat $8 per sq ft for everything, published in ads; add-ons for steps and stem walls

price_points.label: Optional extra to have contents moved

pricing.notes: Premium vs competitors; one competitor about 50% cheaper. Little discounting; 10% off offered for winter interior bookings. Credit card accepted, no financing.

acquisition_channels.details: Meta (mostly Facebook, targeted 55+ males) lead-form ads showing grinding and flake-throwing video (~23 seconds); 80-90%+ of leads. Best ad hook is brother asking 'how much does it cost?' with price stated. Added one qualifying question (interior/garage/exterior/other). Spend about $200/day, doubled to $400/day for second crew; 50-mile radius.

quote.text: it's all basically all meta ads. Yeah. We get some Google traffic. We have a referral program, but it's mostly meta.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Google Local Services Ads used alongside; modest traffic. Not on Thumbtack or Angi.
First three jobs came from friends/church at early-bird discount; $200 referral program produced a ~$30K warehouse job; happy customers recommend contractors.

quote.text: That $200 referral turned into like a $30,000 job cuz we got his mom to do it.
quote.speaker: Mike

acquisition_channels.details: Ask for reviews so the Google Business Profile ranks naturally.

ideas.delivery: Two-person crew (lead at about $35/hr, helper about $25/hr, W2, paid 40 hours/week) grinds floor with a propane 20-inch grinder and vacuum, rolls polyurea base, broadcasts flake, scrapes, applies polyaspartic top coat in a ~10-hour day. Mike does about 1-2 hours/day oversight; brother Luke does phone sales and in-person quotes; two partners are the field experts. Second crew and Des Moines expansion planned.
unit_economics_claims: Materials about $2.06/sq ft (stated as $1.56 base/flake/top plus ~$0.50 misc); overhead about $1/sq ft; labour about $0.80/sq ft; total about $3.90/sq ft versus $8 price
April revenue $60K, May about $69K, profit over 50%
Cost per lead $30 (best ad) to $100; about 20% close rate
One job can yield $3-4K profit in a day
Targeting $1M revenue in first year
ideas.startup_cost: About $22-25K as done (including $10K used U-Haul box truck, ~$1K logo, grinder, vacuum); can trim to $15-20K with electric grinder; under $1,000 theoretically by renting a grinder (~$300/day, ~$1K/week) and doing one job.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: First test job in February 2026 (own garage), three paid early-bird jobs within weeks; paid advertising began March; fully booked from April.

acquisition.how: Meta ad creative copy and budget tuning are done with Claude and can be agent-managed, though video content of real jobs and a human calling leads at once are needed.

onboarding.how: Instant phone call to lead, in-person measuring/quoting and deposit; mostly human salesperson.

delivery.how: Physical grinding, coating and flaking by a two-person crew.

billing.how: 10% deposit then payment on completion via card/Venmo/cheque; invoicing and payment links are easily automated.

support.how: Warranty failures and redo jobs require crews on site; customer questions handled by phone.

uk_applicability.notes: Resin flooring exists in the UK but garages are smaller and less common as a status upgrade, so ticket sizes and demand will be lower, and prices would be in GBP per m2. UK weather and damp slabs matter. No contractor licence needed in general, but insurance applies. Meta lead ads and Google LSA-style channels work; GDPR/PECR needs care for calling leads who opted in (acceptable with consent).

risks: Failed floor from wrong product required a full regrind and redo
Physical, weather and humidity dependent; scheduling slips
Seasonality in winter
Partnering with strangers is risky
Low barriers may attract competition drawn by visual ads
Quality and prep variability per garage; reliable crew hiring
Claims are very recent (2-3 months of data)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews John Cheney, who vibe-coded an AI services business in a weekend, did $180k in six weeks and about $1M in six months, and now has 27 employees. The episode focuses on free customer acquisition: pitching local TV news with a human-interest angle (one segment brought $200-$300k of deals), press releases around partnerships (BYU athletics, Replit), daily authentic social posting, and posting as a whole person. Chris adds his Buc-ee's story, where one cold email to a Texas Monthly reporter led to $180k in sales and a business now making $1M+ net profit a year. Key takeaway: earned media and consistent posting are cheap, asymmetric bets, and fear of others' judgement is the real blocker.

summary: Chris Koerner shows a beginner AI side hustle for garage door repair owners: build an instant quote generator and a job profit tracker with Lovable (no code), plus an after-hours AI voice answering agent in GoHighLevel. He scrapes about 513 Google Maps listings with Outscraper for $111, filters to mobile numbers, cold-texts 50 owners via Straight Text, and gets roughly 40-50% replies and one 'yes' within an hour. He pitches $50 per closed lead with no upfront cost and extrapolates to $100k/month, which is hypothetical. Key takeaway: lead with a low-risk offer, validate with real outreach before building, and use no-code/AI tools to ship fast. Lovable is a channel sponsor and the cold SMS method is illegal in the UK for sole traders.

video.title: How a Regular Guy Started a 1-Person Business with AI

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Phil, a semi-retiree with no coding background who started an AI agency after listening to the podcast. Phil landed a $50,000 six-month retainer with a $1.4B investment firm, a success-based grant-writing app (Grant Craft) for a nonprofit, and a $3,500 + $1,500/month product-launch automation deal for a chiropractor, all from friends and friends of friends. He records discovery meetings and uses Claude for solutions, pricing and contracts, building in Go High Level and Claude Code. Key takeaways: sell to your warm network, listen more than talk, ask for referrals, and productise custom builds.

video.title: 7 Side Hustles For Beginners

summary: Tim Richard lists seven beginner-friendly side hustles he says he has tried or knows about: ShareTown furniture-return resale, Amazon retail arbitrage, Craigslist flipping, finding contract gigs on Indeed, Etsy print-on-demand with Printful and Canva, building a niche content following, and home services. The home services business (starting with junk removal, later outsourced to contractors) is his own and the one he favours, with claimed earnings of $3,000+ a day and seven-figure annual profit. Most other ideas are described in general terms with clips of other people's earnings. The key takeaway is that low-barrier, local, hands-on work like flyering for home services is the easiest start, though it is the least automatable.

video.title: I Told an AI Agent to Make Me Money. It Did.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Brandon Doyle (David AI), who used his OpenClaw AI agent ("Zach Morris", reached via iMessage) to launch three experiments over a month. A custom bedtime-story email subscription (Dreamtales) reached about $300 MRR from ~33 customers on roughly $400 of ads. An agent-built website plus postcard plus cold-call funnel for 350 Utah home-service businesses produced a claimed ~$8K MRR from about 17-20 marketing clients. A Facebook Marketplace/eBay flipping idea was dropped. The key takeaway is that agents did the build and outreach prep, while hard-to-ignore physical postcards and human closing calls drove the results.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews two college-age resellers, Lucas and John, from rural North Carolina/Virginia, who started on eBay selling childhood Legos and thrift-store finds, then moved into bulk consumer electronics. They describe buying 500-unit lots from a European supplier, a bad batch that lost about $4-5k, and diversifying into US suppliers via about 1,000 cold calls and 12,000 emails. They claim six figures of revenue last year and say anyone can make $1,000-5,000 a month with 2-5 hours a week. Key takeaway: reselling starts with low risk (sell your own stuff, thrift, Facebook Marketplace to eBay), but sourcing is the bottleneck and supplier concentration is dangerous.

Margins shrink as you operationalise; early flips return much higher percentages than bulk.
Hot categories rotate; stay tapped into the eBay culture.
Cash flow constrains scale; lacking cash cost them bigger lots.
Reselling is a people business; relationships bring inbound supply offers daily.

video.title: Forget Big Apps. These Tiny Tools Are Making Millions

summary: Chris Koerner explains 'the great unbundling': as Craigslist was split into billion-dollar companies, platforms like Apify, Clay, Zapier and OpenAI can be split into single-purpose tools. He profiles Nico, a former pasta maker turned SDR who vibe-coded a Google Maps lead scraper on an Apify actor. It charges $35/month convertible into credits and reached $3,500 MRR in about 7 months with near-zero costs and word-of-mouth growth. Chris then lists 12+ ideas built the same way, including niche scrapers, Amazon review reports, a Zapier support bot, a micro-influencer finder, an Upwork search tool, a single-feature Clay, a niche 'Zillow' for RV parks or laundromats, and a Shopify-only BuiltWith. His advice is to move fast before the window closes.

video.title: The Beginner-Friendly Claude AI Side Hustle Nobody Talks About

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Ryan Dozer, a solo AI marketer who runs a six-figure SEO/content agency. Dozer explains Claude skills (markdown SOPs for AI agents) and how he packaged about 20-25 of his own into a $99 'Claude Code skill stack' sold from his own site via Stripe, claiming over $3,000 in 30-45 days. He demonstrates an SEO blog-post-writer skill that turns YouTube videos into ranking articles, a LinkedIn scraper skill using Apify, and a vibe-coded marketing OS. Key takeaway: turn the workflows and expertise you already use daily into skills and sell them as digital products, but the numbers are self-reported and the sales path leans on his existing audience.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Mark, a 66-year-old lawyer who designs 'business in a box' ideas, about his nitro iced coffee cart built from a gutted Home Depot tool cart for under ~$1-3k. Using shelf-stable brewed coffee in bag-in-box packs and a nitro tap, he pours 24oz iced coffees in 30 seconds for ~$3 cost and ~$8.50 price, netting $400 at small events, $800-1,200 at festivals and $8,000 at his best two-day event. He also ran beer tap trucks and armoire tap bar rentals, and sets up operators (divorced moms, veterans, visa immigrants) on a ~30% profit split. Key takeaway: strip a product to what customers actually buy, keep capex tiny, and win on location.

video.title: He Spends 1 Hour a Week on This Business

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jay Meldrum, who left corporate professional services to open Swing Cave Golf, a single-bay members-only golf simulator in a Texas strip mall (Allen area). Six months in he has about 28 members on three tiers (USD 175/275/325 per month), roughly USD 7,000 monthly revenue, break-even at about 15 members after three months, and claimed 50-55% net margins. The business is run with 24/7 app-based door access, scheduling software and cameras, with about an hour a week of owner time. Upfront cost is about USD 100K, and he plans a second location and eventual scaling. Takeaway: a low-opex, membership-based, physical-space business can be near-passive once built, but it needs significant capital and a physical site.

summary: William Lindholm describes a cake-sourcing and delivery business that helps companies get sales prospects’ attention with physical gifts. The business began as an automated employee birthday-cake service in Norway, then pivoted in the US to sales campaigns after birthday software proved difficult to sell at scale. William says the new model uses AI agents to find and negotiate with bakeries, while software coordinates large orders and tracks deliveries. The discussion emphasizes attention, measurable sales outcomes, and the need to keep testing which gifts produce meetings and closed sales.

summary: Chris Koerner explains how to start and run a farmer's market (using his wife's kids' market at a shopping centre as the example), then interviews Mike McCoy of Prep Pizza, who sold DIY pizza dough kits at farmer's markets (about $60k in a first summer, part time) before scaling online via Facebook ads to claimed $3-4M of sales. The video also covers other farmer's market products (baked goods, pickles, fresh pasta) and tips such as sampling, choosing in-city markets, and filming content. Key takeaway: farmer's markets are a cheap, fast way to validate a physical food product, and a market organiser can piggyback on a venue that wants footfall.

video.title: The Most Overlooked Side Hustle You Can Start From Home

summary: Chris Koerner visits his neighbour Rayma, a stay-at-home mom of four in Dallas who runs Gifty Gal, a corporate gifting business focused on personalised prospecting gifts for tech sales teams. She started in 2022 with baby shower gifts, grossed about $75k (netting $7,800) in year one, and reached $357k revenue and $119k net in 2025 working about 20 hours a week from home and a shared warehouse. Growth came entirely from referrals and LinkedIn after one LinkedIn post reshared by her husband's network. She explains her pricing (about $100 per prospecting box, 30-50% net margin target, shipping billed separately), wholesale sourcing via Faire and reseller licences, and a four-step framework: connect, collaborate, curate, fulfil.

ideas.business_model: Per-gift product sales with a markup on wholesale-sourced items; shipping billed at cost (client's or negotiated rates); minimum order sizes.
ideas.customer: Sales reps and account managers at corporations, mainly tech companies headquartered in Dallas; also internal team and holiday client gifts
ideas.problem: Prospects and decision makers are swamped with generic gifts and cold calls; sales reps' time is expensive and wasted assembling and shipping gifts themselves
ideas.offer: Gifts tailored to each recipient (alma mater, hobbies, kids' schools) with the client's logo, handwritten cards, premium packaging and full logistics

video.title: The Easiest Way to Actually Make Money With AI

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Corey, who sells a $1,000 'AI assessment' (audit) to small businesses. A voice agent (Annie, built on a voice-AI platform) interviews the owner for 10-20 minutes, another AI agent turns the transcript into a report (Docx to Gamma) recommending off-the-shelf tools, and a follow-up call upsells process optimisation, Zapier/Make automations, custom GPT knowledge systems, CRM setups and speed-to-lead agents at $1.5k-$5k+. Corey then lists tactics for finding customers with no following: local AI meetups, door knocking, free audits for a peer group, and office hours. Key takeaway: you only need to be one step ahead of the client, and a higher-priced audit makes the upsell easier.

summary: Chris Koerner hosts serial entrepreneur Michael Girdley, who pitches about a dozen business ideas picked from a 30-idea list by Koerner's audience poll. They cover an OpenClaw AI-agent persona marketplace, paid AI replicas of famous mentors, an AI-assisted local news site, a curated X magazine, a printed YouTube book for kids, AI skincare, a 'distraction bot' app, admissions negotiation for parents, and AI audits for small businesses. Girdley's strongest recommendation is AI audits as a low-competition entry point that leads to better follow-on AI work. Most of the content is speculative brainstorming with few first-hand numbers.

ideas.name: OpenClaw / agent persona exchange marketplace
ideas.one_liner: A marketplace where creators sell deployable AI-agent 'personas' (marketing manager, sales rep) and the exchange takes a cut.
ideas.business_model: Marketplace commission on persona sales (subscription or licence); creators sell free/open or closed-source versions
ideas.customer: Business owners who want ready-made AI agents that act like employees; creators who want to sell their own versions
ideas.problem: Hard to find pre-built, trusted AI agents for specific roles such as cold email or marketing
ideas.offer: A searchable exchange with filters, tech stack and approximate token costs for each persona, like an eBay for agents

video.title: The Most Passive Online Side Hustle I've Ever Seen

summary: Chris Koerner argues that simple AI-vibe-coded calculator or tool websites (paycheck, calorie, mortgage, etc.) can earn passive ad and email-lead income because they capture large search volume. He cites big examples (paycheck calculator, calorie calculator, Omni Calculator) and his own pet cremation directory calculators. He then builds an AI token cost calculator in Hostinger Horizons in about 6 minutes, picks the niche with Google Trends, adds email gating and AdSense, and publishes it. Key takeaway: build many cheap niche tool sites, validate with trends and keyword data, and monetise beyond AdSense with email capture and lead sales. The video is sponsored by Hostinger, so the ease claims are promotional.

speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; serial entrepreneur who says he has started over 80 businesses.

ideas.name: AI-built niche calculator website (AI token cost calculator)
ideas.one_liner: Vibe-code a simple calculator site around a growing search term, monetise with AdSense and email capture, and leave it running.
ideas.business_model: Ads (Google AdSense), email list monetisation (newsletter, affiliate links), possible lead sales.
ideas.customer: People searching Google or AI for a calculator; in the demo, vibe coders and people building with AI tools.
ideas.problem: People want a quick answer (e.g. what AI prompts cost in tokens) and find it hard to work out themselves.
ideas.offer: Free calculator that estimates AI model cost from input and output tokens, with a token counter and tips to cut usage; results unlock after entering an email.

pricing.model: Free to users; revenue from ads and email value

price_points.label: AdSense at about 10,000 page views a month: 30 to 100 USD
Claimed value of an email address

pricing.notes: Hypothetical figures only; the demo site has no revenue yet.

acquisition_channels.details: Pick high or growing search-volume keywords (core and long-tail) using Semrush, Ahrefs or an AI tool, check Google Trends, and add SEO content such as token-reduction tips.

quote.text: Best tool sites solve a very specific problem that have high andor growing search volume.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Site is built by prompting Hostinger Horizons (AI app builder), published on a custom domain, and needs about an hour a week afterwards (claimed). Further calculators can be cloned from the same template.
unit_economics_claims: AdSense at 10,000 monthly page views yields about 30 to 100 USD a month
Email at 1% of 10,000 visitors gives 100 emails, hypothetically about 1,000 USD a month at 10 USD each
Hostinger starter plan allows up to 25 websites
ideas.startup_cost: Hostinger starter plan, 12-month, 10% off with code; the domain is about a cent for year one or a free .cloud domain; the transcript states no total. Builder credits used: 4 of 70 for the month.

acquisition.how: Organic SEO traffic is inbound; keyword research and content can be done by agents. Rankings take time and are uncertain.

onboarding.how: There are no customers to onboard; the visitor just uses the tool.

delivery.how: A static or serverless calculator runs unattended once built; occasional price-data updates can be agent-driven.

billing.how: Ad networks pay out automatically; there are no invoices.

support.how: Low support needs; occasional bug reports or data corrections can be handled by an agent.

uk_applicability.notes: Works in the UK. Email capture needs UK GDPR and PECR consent for marketing, and cookie consent is required for AdSense. UK-relevant calculators (tax, mortgage, student loan) are available. UK ad RPMs may differ.

Rankings are uncertain and AI search or Google AI answers may cut calculator traffic
Easy to copy, so competition is rising

Token pricing data goes stale

video.title: He Can't Code but His AI Agents Make Him $5K/Month

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Vadim, an 18-year-old non-coder who vibe-coded Vugola, an all-in-one clipping, scheduling and captioning SaaS, using Claude Code, Supabase, Vercel and GitHub. He claims $5K revenue in 30 days at ~80% margin, with 267 paying users on $9/$39/$99 plans, acquired mainly via Twitter after Reddit/X outreach by an OpenClaw agent. He also describes running a small team of Hermes agents (CEO, marketing, growth, coding, support) and shares prompting tips, PostHog analytics, Paperclip, and mind-mapping for niche research. Key takeaway: a solo founder can build and run a niche SaaS with AI agents cheaply, but the numbers are self-reported and the product is still in beta.

summary: Chris Koerner builds GovDealFinder, a simple search front end over SAM.gov federal contract listings, using Replit Agent 4 with a Claude-written prompt and the free SAM.gov API, in about four minutes. He adds email alerts for new contracts matching saved filters, SEO blog posts, an eligibility quiz, a generated pitch deck, and publishes on a $12 domain. The pitch: the US government spent $834 billion on contracts last year, about $200 billion is reserved for small businesses, and SAM.gov is clunky. video.title: This AI Finds Cheap Products You Can Sell for 5x More

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates going from a physical product idea to a sourced product in one sitting, using the AI sourcing agent Accio (transcribed 'Axio'). He validates demand for a discreet 'porch pirate' parcel box via Google Trends, searches Accio in natural language, generates a tech pack, and compares supplier prices to Amazon listings. He claims a $27 sourced box sells for $143 on Amazon, about 75-80% gross margin and 20-30% net after shipping and fees. The video is sponsored by Accio, so the takeaway is that sourcing and validation tools make starting a physical product business faster, but the numbers are an unverified back-of-envelope demo.

video.title: They Banned My $35K/Month Page So I Started a Business

summary: Host Chris Koerner describes losing a Facebook page that had generated substantial income, then launching Plans of Grandeur by selling previously unpublished creator training to his newsletter. He tests prices and email formats with randomized subscriber groups, takes payment through Stripe, and later organizes the material in a community. He reports that the launch generated tens of thousands of dollars in revenue and profit, while presenting his process as a repeatable way to sell useful content to an existing audience. The video also discusses his former creator consulting, Facebook monetization, newsletter tutorials, and small-list sales of courses and events.

ideas.offer: Videos, guides, documents, and tracking spreadsheets from Koerner's Google Drive, later organized in a community. Buyers receive future tactical content and 12 recorded AMAs.

pricing.model: One-time lifetime payment; presale price was tested against two price points, then the $97 price was selected. A higher full launch price was planned.

price_points.label: A/B test and selected presale price
Planned full price on launch day

pricing.notes: Koerner described the $97 presale as 67% off the planned $291 price. He later chose $97 after testing $47 and $97. The offer was described as lifetime and non-recurring.

acquisition_channels.details: Emailed active subscribers from Koerner's newsletter. He randomized the list, tagged and segmented test groups, excluded unsubscribed subscribers and people who had already received the test emails, and sent the winning offer to the remaining list.

quote.text: I'm going to take a sample of my entire email list and launch not just like test, but launch the business with a Stripe link to pay uh at one price to sample A and then at another price to sample B.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: The video explains the offer and directs viewers to a special link in its description or pinned comment.

quote.text: Also, by the way, if you're watching this, I've got a special link in the description where you can get lower price.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Initially, the Stripe payment link redirected buyers to a Google Drive folder. Koerner later had his business partner download and organize the files into a Skool community, then invited buyers. He also recorded Loom videos, including a welcome walkthrough and a video showing the charity donation.
unit_economics_claims: Koerner reported $8,300 in revenue after 111 transactions and said costs were almost all profit, aside from Stripe transaction fees.
He later reported $23,000 in nearly pure profit after the full-list email and prior price tests.
He said total net profit across the video was between $30,000 and $40,000.
tools: Beehiiv for the newsletter, subscriber segments, tags, and email campaigns
Google Sheets for randomizing and dividing the email list
Stripe for one-time payment links, transaction analytics, and payment processing
Google Drive for hosting the original training materials
Skool for organizing the content and community
Loom for welcome and donation videos
Claude for reviewing A/B test results and creating a logo
ChatGPT for generating the community description
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Koerner bought the domain for $11.28 per year during setup; other setup costs were not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Koerner says the first $97 sale arrived in under two hours from the idea. He reports sending the first test email at about 12:30 and getting the first sale at 12:41.

acquisition.how: An opted-in newsletter can be segmented, emailed, and measured with software. UK marketing rules still require a valid basis to email subscribers and functioning unsubscribe handling.

onboarding.how: Stripe can take payment and redirect buyers to the materials; tagging and invitations can be automated. The transcript describes manual setup and some manual community invitations.

delivery.how: Digital files and recorded training can be delivered automatically. New material, AMAs, and community upkeep still require human work.

billing.how: Stripe payment links can collect one-time payments without manual invoicing. Refunds and exceptions may need a human.

support.how: A digital library can answer routine questions, but promised AMAs, community discussion, and refund requests need human involvement.

uk_applicability.notes: Digital training, email sales to an appropriately opted-in list, and online payment work in the UK. The founder would need to follow UK consumer, privacy, and email-marketing rules and make the offer's lifetime and support terms clear.

risks: The offer relies on an existing audience and trust; results may not transfer to a founder without a newsletter or established reputation.
A lifetime-content promise and 12 AMAs create ongoing delivery and support obligations.
The video presents short-term A/B results from a finite list; delayed purchases changed the relative results over time.
Email marketing in the UK requires an appropriate legal basis, accurate subscriber records, and working unsubscribe handling.
The host calls the product almost pure profit, but support, platform fees, refunds, and ongoing content work can reduce margins.

tactics.name: Randomize the list before an email price test
steps: Export active subscribers and put the addresses in Google Sheets.

tactics.name: Test price with the same email and different payment links
steps: Create the same one-time offer at $47 and $97.

Compare the revenue and conversion results, and allow time for higher-priced purchases to arrive.
Repeat tests when results are uncertain before sending the selected offer to the rest of the list.

tactics.name: Reduce checkout friction
steps: Use a direct payment link and avoid asking for information already held in the subscriber list.

Exclude prior test groups from later campaigns to avoid sending the same offer repeatedly.

video.title: He Asked AI To Make Money. It Did.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Robbie, a non-technical operations employee who gave an OpenClaw AI agent ('Ron') $100 and 90 days to make money, inspired by the 2023 HustleGPT experiment. Ron's first idea (SWOT analysis gigs on Fiverr) failed for lack of visibility, but Ron scraped 200 TikTok comments from people wanting their own Ron. Robbie then launched 'AI Co-Founder Club', hosted containerised OpenClaw agents on rented Contabo servers, took $10 pre-orders and converted them to $29/month memberships. He claims about $8.4k MRR after 13 days with ~$2.6k monthly costs. Key takeaway: document the build publicly, validate with paid pre-orders, and sell to the audience your experiment attracts.

video.title: He Turns Abandoned Driving Ranges Into Cash Machines

summary: Chris Koerner visits Golf Ranch in Richardson, Dallas, whose founding team (ex-Topgolf and long-time paid-ads operator) buys dated or abandoned driving ranges and modernises them. They upgraded ball and mat quality based on customer surveys, added covered bays, lights to midnight, music, string lights and a putting green, and replaced prepaid bucket cards with a $20/month Ranch Pass membership (40% off buckets); they now have 8,000 members across four sites and claim an LTV:CAC of about 10. Volume at this site went from about 3.5 million to 12 million balls a year. The key takeaway is that an old, underserved industry with a low bar can be won by listening to customers, a membership loop, loss-leader amenities and modern digital marketing; the goal is 50 sites and 100,000 members.

video.title: How to Make $1.6K/Day on Facebook Marketplace

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Matt (Jackson, Michigan), a former high school math teacher who started flipping couches, appliances and church pews on Facebook Marketplace/Craigslist, then moved to riding and zero-turn lawnmowers. He claims $20-30K profit in his first summer, quit teaching, built a helper network (drivers, a mechanic, 'Family of Flippers'), sourced volume from dealers who dislike used stock, and now runs a Toro/Bad Boy etc. equipment dealership with a best month of $1.1M. The episode is heavy on tactics: speed to lead, deposits, negotiation (make the seller name the number first), outsourcing driving first, and calling dealers for under-advertised used inventory. Key takeaway: the edge is buying underpriced at speed and selling at market value, not fixing items.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews David (Fort Wayne, Indiana), a 'multipreneur' running several small rental businesses. He details a tote (moving box) rental business sold via a realtor gifting subscription, a travel-trailer (RV) rental business that made about $7,000 net in its first season, and a side-hustle recording/video studio. The takeaway is that small rental businesses need little capital, reuse the same asset repeatedly, and can be validated by asking existing operators and using marketplaces as lead-gen before moving customers to your own site.

video.title: How I Use Web Scraping to Find Products That Sell for 20x the Price

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates how to use the Oxylabs web scraper API (his sponsor) to scrape Amazon best-seller lists in three categories (pet accessories, household/health, children's education books), then analyse them in Google Sheets and Claude to find products with strong sales rank but low review counts. He then finds near-identical products on Alibaba via image search and works through landed-cost and Amazon fee maths (about 30% net margin claimed on a cat feeder). He adds extra screening tactics: one-star test, fee-tier size shrinking, variations, rating distribution, Google Trends, Amazon Choice badges. Key takeaway: pick Amazon products by data (rank vs review mismatch) rather than personal interest, but the margin maths is rough and the evidence is promotional.

video.title: The Easiest $3K/Day Business Nobody Is Talking About

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Sariah (27, Utah), who started Memory Magnets Co with under $1,000 in 2024 after her husband's low pay and second job left the family broke. She sells custom photo magnets online, at markets and as an on-the-spot wedding/event service, and sells magnet-making machine kits plus refill supplies and courses. She claims $1.63M online revenue in her first full year (about $600K profit), a $233K best month and a $100.5K first six-figure month after six months. Key takeaway: a simple, high-margin physical product plus a service at price-insensitive events (weddings), marketed through short-form video, grew fast, and teaching others to copy the model became a second revenue line.

video.title: The Most Underrated Way to Make $50K/Month

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Matt and Joanie, who started Sonoma Strong Hauling junk removal in Sonoma County when Matt was 35 and just out of jail and rehab. Starting part-time with a pickup and a free Craigslist post, they did $87k in year one at ~70% margin and now do $50k/month at ~35% net with a small crew. The episode focuses on free, old-school marketing: candy dishes at every real estate office, friending 2,000+ realtors on Facebook, daily local Facebook group posts, bandit signs, partner referrals and YouTube. Key takeaway: scrappy local relationship marketing plus professional branding can fill a low-capital service business, and growth spending should follow demand.

video.title: Make $500k/Year with One Email a Week

summary: Chris Koerner has Tyler Denk, co-founder of Beehiiv and early Morning Brew employee, walk through starting a newsletter from zero on Beehiiv (website, template, welcome automation, recommendations, Boost, magic links) and monetising it. Tyler's own 120,000-subscriber weekly side-project newsletter, Big Desk Energy, has generated about $500k: $5-7k per sponsored send, ~$80k per $10,000-a-head founder mastermind in Costa Rica, and $10-25k from Boost. Both argue niche lists (even 500-5,000 high-value readers) can earn well through sponsorships, events or consulting, and that paid acquisition at ~$1.45-2.50 per subscriber becomes a flywheel when Boost/recommendation income and sponsorships return more. Chris shows how he segments his list and uses surveys to build a media kit. The episode is effectively promotional for Beehiiv.

video.title: Now is the Best Time to Make Money with Content (AI Tutorial)

summary: Chris Koerner argues now is a great time to earn from content inspired by other creators' content in any niche. He walks through building an n8n workflow on a Hostinger VPS (about $5/month) that reads YouTube channel RSS feeds on a schedule, appends the videos to a Google Sheet and emails a digest. Setup covers the Google Cloud Console APIs and OAuth consent, an RSS Read node, Google Sheets and Gmail nodes, and an Aggregate node to fix email spam. He suggests the tool could be resold, for example as a $30/month competitor-monitoring email to YouTubers, or sold as n8n templates. The video is promotional for Hostinger.

tactics.name: Build a YouTube competitor-tracking digest in n8n
steps: Buy a Hostinger VPS with n8n preinstalled
In Google Cloud Console create a project, enable the Gmail and Google Sheets APIs, configure the OAuth consent screen with external audience and test users
Add Gmail read/send/modify and Sheets read/write scopes
In n8n add a Schedule trigger, then an RSS Read node per channel
Get each channel's RSS URL from the page source by searching for RSS, which avoids third-party sites that harvest your email
Append publish date, channel name and title to a Google Sheet
Add an Aggregate node (titles, links) before the Gmail node so you get one digest email, not one per video
Limit to the latest 10 items per channel and schedule daily

quote.text: I'm going to add a node right here between RSS and Gmail. Hit the plus. It's going to be called aggregate.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

steps: Pick a niche and identify top creators

video.title: She Makes $1k/Day Sending Letters

summary: Hannah describes how she started Tiny Post, a monthly snail-mail club, after building a neighborhood farmers market in Austin. She grew the club through TikTok and other organic social posts, then hired help to pack and mail its physical contents. The conversation also covers related letter-club niches, direct-mail ideas, and ways to extend the product. Its strongest lesson for a founder seeking an agent-run business is that the customer-facing storytelling can use software, but making and mailing the distinctive product still takes substantial human work.

speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office.

speakers.description: Founder of the Tiny Project and Tiny Post in Austin.

ideas.name: Tiny Post snail-mail club
ideas.one_liner: Send subscribers a monthly envelope of original art, a recipe, stickers, a paper goodie, and a personal letter.
ideas.business_model: Monthly recurring subscription for a physical mailer.

ideas.problem: Subscribers want an affordable way to receive art and a personal, tangible connection.
ideas.offer: A monthly 1 oz envelope with Hannah's art print/postcard, recipe card, usually two stickers, a surprise paper goodie, and a personal letter. The contents change monthly.

acquisition_channels.details: Hannah posted consistently on TikTok, sharing why she started the club, its connection to the farmers market, and the product. A video of her telling her husband about the idea later reached a large audience. She also said unboxing posts from subscribers helped spread the word.

quote.text: And I charged $11 for it. And I just posted it on TikTok. And the first month I got 50 people.
quote.speaker: Hannah

quote.speaker: Hannah

ideas.delivery: Hannah creates the art and letter, coordinates recipes and paper goods, and packs the envelopes with family and other helpers. The group batches the work during one week each month and ships the letters through the post. Hannah says the personal handling is part of what makes it feel special.
unit_economics_claims: Hannah said postage was 78 cents per envelope and estimated the other hard costs brought the total to about $3.
The host estimated gross margin at about 70% before labor.
Hannah said six people could pack about 1,000 letters in two and a half hours.
Hannah estimated subscriber turnover at about 5% monthly, versus her 10% planning assumption.
The host and guest discussed about 4,100 current subscribers and nearly $50,000 in monthly recurring revenue; the host estimated $25,000–$30,000 monthly profit and Hannah confirmed about $25,000.
ideas.startup_cost: The host described startup costs as next to nothing. Hannah did not give a specific startup-cost figure.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Hannah said she had the idea on a Tuesday and started about a week later. She reported 50 subscribers in the first month.

acquisition.how: Agents could help edit posts, schedule content, answer routine questions, and track referral sources. The most effective content depends on Hannah's personal story, so human input remains important.

onboarding.how: A signup form, payment flow, confirmation, and address collection can be automated, with human review for exceptions.

delivery.how: The art and writing are personal, and people physically assemble and mail the envelopes. Software can manage lists and print labels but cannot replace the core production work described.

billing.how: Subscription payments, renewals, failed-payment notices, and cancellations can largely run through subscription software with occasional checks.

support.how: Agents can answer shipping, account, and product questions from a help guide; personal complaints or creative feedback need a human.

uk_applicability.notes: A UK founder could sell and post a similar monthly letter using UK postal services. The product and subscription model do not depend on US-only rules or platforms.

risks: Packing, postage, and product weight create recurring physical work; envelopes over the 1 oz limit require more postage.
A viral post can create more demand than a small team can fulfill; Hannah closed signups and used a waitlist after feeling overwhelmed.
A waitlist form that does not disclose the price can attract low-intent signups; Hannah said she made this mistake.
The host's gross-margin estimate excludes labor, which Hannah identified as a major cost.
Adding advertisements could weaken the mission and customer trust; Hannah declined an advertising offer for that reason.
A monthly physical product is exposed to postal delays, damage, postage changes, and production errors.

tactics.name: Use a personal story as the content
steps: Explain why the product exists and what personal experience led to it.
Show the work and the process rather than only making a direct sales pitch.
Use comments and questions to explain the product to people who have not encountered it before.
Keep publishing and learn from how the audience responds.

video.title: How to Buy Big Things with Little Money

summary: Chris Koerner explains ways to acquire property, businesses, and other valuable assets with little upfront cash, drawing on his own purchases and negotiations. He focuses on seller financing structures, building trust with sellers, staying flexible about the asset, and documenting a project publicly to attract customers or investors. His examples include real estate, short-term rentals, RV parks, and a landscaping business. The main takeaway is to reduce risk for the seller, negotiate terms creatively, and be ready to walk away if the deal does not work on the numbers.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; shares personal acquisition experience and examples.

ideas.name: Buy businesses and assets with little cash using creative financing
ideas.one_liner: Acquire a business or asset by negotiating seller financing, flexible terms, and a relationship of trust.
ideas.business_model: Acquire an existing business or asset, improve or operate it, then earn from its cash flow or resale.
ideas.customer: Sellers of businesses, real estate, or other assets; the buyer is the founder or operator.
ideas.problem: The buyer wants an asset but lacks the cash for a conventional down payment or financing terms.
ideas.offer: A purchase proposal that adjusts the down payment, timing, payment schedule, collateral, or future profit share to suit both parties.

pricing.model: Negotiated purchase price and financing terms.
pricing.notes: Terms depend on the asset and seller. The transcript gives several hypothetical structures rather than one standard price.

acquisition_channels.details: Find owners in an asset class, build a relationship, visit in person more than once, follow up, and explain how the buyer can add value.

quote.text: Visit him in person multiple times, follow up with him, bring your spouse and kids if that's the case.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Document the project on free social platforms to build an audience and attract prospective customers or investors.

quote.text: If you bring the world along with you through these free media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, Tik Tok, whatever, then you can skip the line.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The buyer operates or improves the acquired asset. The seller may receive installments, interest, a balloon payment, future appreciation, or another negotiated form of consideration.
unit_economics_claims: Chris says he bought an $800,000 business with $50,000 down.
The transcript gives hypothetical buy-and-resell math for a landscaping business.
tools: ChatGPT for generating alternative financing structures
Banks for conventional or alternative loan options
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; the purpose is to reduce the amount of cash required upfront.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; depends on the asset and financing terms.

acquisition.how: Finding and persuading an owner depends on trust and often repeated personal contact; software can assist with research but cannot replace the relationship.

onboarding.how: Document collection and deal administration can use software, but parties and advisers must agree and review the contract.

delivery.how: Operating a purchased business or physical asset requires human oversight and may involve physical work.

billing.how: Scheduled payments can be automated, but payment terms and servicing need human setup and monitoring.

support.how: Seller relations and operational issues require human judgement and communication.

uk_applicability.notes: Seller financing and negotiated purchase terms can work in the UK, but legal, tax, lending, and property rules differ and need local advice.

risks: A balloon payment may become due before the buyer can refinance or sell; default can return the asset to the seller.
A seller with a second lien position may recover little or nothing if a senior lender is paid first.
Interest-only payments do not reduce principal and interest may compound.
A lease-to-own or master lease can leave the buyer with operating risk and no ownership if the option is not exercised.
Borrowing from friends and family can damage valuable personal relationships.
Do not become emotionally attached to a deal; be willing to walk away.

quotes.text: your best shot of being able to buy something big with little money is seller financing, preferably as close to 100% as possible.
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

quotes.text: You've got to be willing to build a relationship of trust.

tactics.name: Document the project publicly
steps: Start a social account before launch, even with no followers.

Study other creators in the niche: hooks, music, posting frequency, asset type, and comments.
Paste comment text into ChatGPT to identify themes that may resonate with viewers.

tactics.name: Broaden the asset search and build seller trust

Look for an owner who is willing to get to know you and whom you also like.

Offer value, compliment the property sincerely, visit more than once, and follow up.

video.title: People Are Selling One Prompt Websites for $1K+ (Full Tutorial)

summary: A sponsored tutorial in which Chris Koerner uses the AI website builder Wegic (transcribed as Ouijic/Weedic) to build a site for his planned Secret Pickleball club, with court booking, leaderboard and members-only merch, in about two and a half minutes, then a Dallas pizza restaurant site with payment buttons, menu and a lead-capture chatbot in about one minute. He pitches it as a way to save $3-5k on a designer or to start a web design agency selling sites for thousands of dollars. His advice is to pick an industry you understand, dig into owners' booking and lead-handling headaches with why/how/who questions, and price on value rather than time. Evidence is promotional: the video is an ad for Wegic.

video.title: This Business Makes Vending Machines Look Dumb

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Forest, a 34-year-old former Pepsi/Coke/Bang merchandiser and beverage brand rep. He bought a failed pastry route for $15k, grew it to about $800k a year and sold it in two parts for about $185k. He then moved to Billings, Montana and started a small-distributor business selling jerky, candy and novelty snacks to independent gas stations and grocery stores. He reports about 95 accounts, roughly $50k a month in sales, 30% net margin and one lost account. The takeaway is that a hands-on, relationship-based route business that merchandises and buys back unsold stock, using local products, net-10 customer terms and net-14 to net-30 supplier terms, can start with very little capital. It is physical, driving-heavy work, not agent-run.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; owner of Texas Snacks gas station business, wholesale and retail experience

speakers.name: Forest
speakers.description: Owner of Cough Tree Wholesale (name as transcribed), a snack and jerky distributor in Billings, Montana; ex-Pepsi/Coke/Bang merchandiser and former pastry route owner

ideas.name: Independent-store jerky and candy micro-distributor (merchandising route)
ideas.one_liner: Drive a route to independent gas stations, grocery and hardware stores every 14 days, selling jerky, candy and novelty snacks by the case, merchandising the shelf and buying back unsold stock.
ideas.business_model: Wholesale resale margin: buy from manufacturers, mark up 30-45%, sell by the case to stores on net-10 terms. No service fee.
ideas.customer: Independent gas stations, small grocery stores, hardware stores, lumber yards, liquor stores and auto parts stores, mostly rural; small regional chains (e.g. 8-store and 20-store accounts).
ideas.problem: Big wholesalers drop product and leave, with no upselling or relationship, no regional or local products, and store owners carry the mental load of ordering and forecasting inventory. Out-of-stocks and outdated stock are not bought back.
ideas.offer: Visit every other week, place the order, merchandise and rotate the shelf, take over whole sections (e.g. jerky), supply products the big wholesaler does not carry (especially local brands), buy back credits on unsold or outdated items, and supply free manufacturer racks and displays. Positioned as an addition to the store's existing wholesaler.

pricing.model: Per-case wholesale with 30-45% markup over cost, net-10 customer terms

price_points.unit: per delivery at best grocery store
price_points.label: best grocery account

price_points.unit: per jerky case (some cases over $100; about $30 profit)
price_points.label: case price

pricing.notes: Markup 30-45%, so the example $1,000 order yields about $350-400 gross profit. Net margin about 30% when owner-operated, about 20% if staff run it. Sells by the case only.

acquisition_channels.details: Walks into independent stores with the product in the truck or trailer, a price sheet and a fun one-pager, and offers to fetch the display on the spot. Re-visits non-buyers every other Tuesday; the second follow-up is usually when they say yes. Early close rate about 4 in 10.

quote.text: you give them the one pager that has some fun photos. And I always tell them like, "Hey, let me go grab the product now."
quote.speaker: Forest

acquisition_channels.details: Relationship-based; owners help other local businesses. Existing accounts and regional chains bring more stores (e.g. a 30-store owner, a 25-store regional account, a four-store chain asking him to bring in a brand).

Manufacturers want distributors; one jerky brand sent a salesman to open stores for him. Called competitor owners for market insight and brand intros. Used Google to find cool local or non-saturated brands and pitched them using a list of about 50 independent stores.
Used Google Maps and satellite or street view to find stores that look independent, ignoring fuel branding like Shell or BP, and built the route list from that.

ideas.delivery: Owner drives a pickup with an enclosed trailer (now a box truck) 10-12 stops a day, about 6-8 hours, in a radius of about 2.5 hours around Billings. He is salesperson, driver, merchandiser and order-taker. Monday is warehouse day: pallets are received by staff at a local storage facility and the family helps put away stock. Invoices are made in a cheap app and printed. Buy-backs are rare because he picks products himself.

Gross margin about 35-40%, net margin about 30% owner-operated
Warehouse about $1,400/month for 1,500 sq ft; earlier two storage units about $500/month
One account lost in about 16 months
Full route could gross about $800k/yr with a $50-70k/yr driver

acquisition.how: Door-to-door walk-in sales to store owners is in-person and relationship-based. Agents could help build target lists from Maps and manage follow-up schedules, but the selling is human.

uk_applicability.notes: Independent convenience stores, farm shops, garages and pubs exist in the UK, and cash-and-carry or van-sales models are established. Selling to stores is B2B, so PECR is not a barrier to visits, but cold email or call to sole traders needs care. Prices would be in GBP with local British brands.

video.title: How to Make $120k/Year with An Army of AI Influencers

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates creating an AI influencer in Higgsfield's AI Influencer Studio, generating videos (including from his own recorded video) and posting to Instagram. He shows Higgsfield's 'Earn' programme that pays creators for posts with a specific caption, and gives per-thousand-view payout ranges for Facebook, YouTube, TikTok. Key takeaway: faceless AI-influencer content is easy to start, but platform payouts are small and the bigger money is driving traffic off-platform (newsletter, affiliates, products). video.title: How I Make $35k/Month With Other People's Content (Legally)

summary: Chris Koerner shows how he makes $10k-$35k/month profit on Facebook's creator program by adding commentary to viral content (claimed fair use), spending about 3 hours a week. He walks through sourcing reels on a fresh Instagram account, scripting with Gemini, editing green-screen overlays in CapCut, posting natively everywhere, and tagging creators. He funnels Facebook traffic to a Beehiiv newsletter (96k to 250k subscribers in a year) and monetizes signups via SparkLoop. A sample video critiques a junk removal claim and lays out a no-truck bootstrap plan.
