video.title: He Watched This Channel and Started a $2,600/Week Side Hustle

summary: Tim describes testing a mobile RC construction play experience at fairs and private events, then preparing a permanent store with construction and rock-crawling zones. He shares session prices, event costs, startup spending, early sales, and the software he built in Replit to manage sessions and other operations. The store is a larger, less-proven expansion, with memberships and an outdoor course planned. The main takeaway is that event testing helped him learn about demand and operations before committing to a permanent location, though several store projections remain estimates.

video.title: 40 Ways to Make $400,000 from Unwanted Land

summary: Chris Koerner presents dozens of ways to earn money from unwanted or underused land, using examples from his property and businesses he has seen. Ideas range from camping, storage and rentals to food, trees, construction, equipment and land resale. He repeatedly recommends testing demand before making large investments, using existing marketplaces, and finding ways to repurpose low-cost assets. Many examples are US-specific, rely on physical work, or are anecdotes about other operators rather than independently verified results.

video.title: How to Get Your First Service Clients Paying Tens of Thousands

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jamison, a former private-equity professional who launched West Coast Decks in Southern California with no trade experience. He closed $60,000 of jobs in month one using paid lead services, and says he reached just under $1M in year one and now does $4-8M a year. The video is a tactical playbook for launching a high-ticket home service business: pick a low-decision-count, high-order-value niche, invest in branding early, respond to leads in seconds, hire a well-paid VA, cultivate referrals from adjacent trades via social media, and bid at 50% gross margin (2x COGS).

speakers.description: Founder of West Coast Decks (Southern California), ex-Wall Street/private equity

ideas.name: West Coast Decks (premium deck building)
ideas.one_liner: High-ticket deck design and build company in Southern California, started with no trade experience using strong branding and fast lead response.
ideas.business_model: Per-job project sales, bid at about 2x cost of service (50% gross margin)
ideas.customer: Southern California homeowners wanting new decks or deck repair; also referrals via landscapers, roofers and other trades
ideas.problem: Homeowners want a deck built or repaired by a trustworthy, professional contractor rather than a handyman; the market is short of good providers
ideas.offer: Design and installation of decks (wood or composite, railings, optional lighting and outdoor kitchens), sold in a short one-meeting close

pricing.model: Project-based quote; cost of labor and materials x2
pricing.notes: Early pricing was admittedly too low, which helped close the first jobs and gather social proof.

acquisition_channels.details: Paid lead services at launch (Angie's List, HomeAdvisor; today Thumbtack, TaskRabbit, Angie). Deck repair leads about $60 and deck build leads about $120. Respond within 30 seconds, site visit within a day, proposal within another day.
Posts daily on Instagram and Facebook plus an email newsletter; consistent branding and profiles on Google, Yelp, Houzz, BBB and Chamber of Commerce.

Instagram-driven referrals from other trades (mostly landscapers, roofers) said to produce about $400k in year one and $600k in year two; also meets lumber yards and supplier sales reps in person who send leads.
No ads for the first 3 years; PPC, Google LSA and Meta ads are a 2026 initiative.

ideas.delivery: Installed physically by crews; California in-house versus subcontractors is tricky, he says either works if managed well. Installs about half a million sq ft of decking per year.
unit_economics_claims: Closed $60k in 3 jobs in month one for about $1,500 of lead spend
Bid at 50% gross margin (2x COGS) to reach about 15% net
Year one revenue just under $1M; now $4-8M per year
ideas.startup_cost: $15,000 set aside as working capital; branding under about $3,000
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: First month ($60k closed within about 3 days of leads)

acquisition.how: Lead-marketplace purchases, ads and social posting can be tooled, but supplier/trade relationship building and rapid human responses drive results.

onboarding.how: Site visits and quote meetings are in person; design decisions made with the client.

delivery.how: Physical construction work by crews.

billing.how: Invoicing and deposits can be handled by software, with change-order enforcement by humans.

support.how: Homeowner expectation management needs a human.

uk_applicability.notes: Home-improvement decking works in the UK, but lead platforms differ (Checkatrade, MyBuilder, Bark), the climate and regulations differ, and he would need real trade crews.

risks: Asymmetric downside: costs only compress after the bid
Customer expectation mismatches
Pricing too low early
Key-man risk until about $7-8M revenue
Need to respond instantly to leads

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates building a niche CRM micro-app for independent pool service operators using only AI, with no coding. He uses Claude to pick a growing niche, then compares Claude Code, Replit and ChatGPT on the same prompt: Claude Code built it in about 2 minutes and was best, Replit took about 16 minutes, ChatGPT was fast but gave code without a preview. He then runs a back-of-envelope market sizing (79,000 US pool businesses, 1,000 customers at $20-$100/month) and outlines customer-finding methods: Facebook groups for feedback, Gummy Search for Reddit pain points, Claude deep research, Google Trends, scraping and cold outreach, and Facebook custom-audience ads. summary: Chris Koerner tests a disc golf 'ace challenge' inspired by a New Zealand floating golf green that reportedly nets $500k a year: players pay for throws and win $1,000 for a hole-in-one. In a Dallas park, security stopped him charging or paying out, so revenue was $0. At DFW Disc Golf in Arlington, with proceeds going to the owner's homeless charity, players threw from 95 feet and one skilled player aced it after about 180 shots, with $780 in fees against the $1,000 prize. Key takeaway: skill-challenge businesses are a statistics problem, so test for free to measure hit rates by distance and skill, then price accordingly and partner with tournaments and shops.

video.title: How I Turned A Gas Station Visit Into A Multi-Million Dollar Business

summary: Chris Koerner walks through the Buc-ee's mega gas station that supplies his Texas Snacks business, where he and his partner spend millions a year at full retail and resell Buc-ee's-branded snacks and merch online via Shopify. He gives store vs online prices (shirts 18 to ~33-35 USD, Beaver Nuggets 5 to 9 USD, jerky only ~40% markup) and explains the logistics: pre-ordered pallets, box truck, warehouse, listing and email blasts. He recounts the origin: spending ~3,000 USD on one of everything because Buc-ee's did not sell online, then doing 160,000 USD in month one. Key takeaway: the gap is real but margins are thin, competition is heavy and the business depends on the brand's goodwill.

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates a 'validate before you build' workflow: he polls 100 US small business owners via PickFu on which website feature they'd pay for, then uses the Mocha vibe-coding app to build an appointment booking widget (BookFlow) in under 20 minutes. Appointment booking tied with chatbot for first place; ChatGPT analysis of the written responses suggests bundling booking, forms, price calculator and a chatbot layer, leading with scheduling in ads. Key takeaway: poll your target buyer first, mine the free-text answers with an LLM, then prototype quickly with AI and sell before fully building. Mocha is described as a 'friend of the pod' (promotional link).

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Will Cannon, who built the B2B lead-data SaaS UpLead and the e-signature SaaS Signaturely. Will describes going from a failed mortgage company to selling email lists, then an agency, then UpLead (about $1M ARR in year one, cold email plus SEO). He then explains how he cloned the e-signature category by mining G2 reviews, building a 'stupid simple' product and proving he could get customers before building. The pair also pitch a free vertical CRM monetised through payments and payroll, and both stress selling before building and that 10k a month is a life-changing target.

video.title: Stop Wasting Money on Bad Ideas. Do This Instead.

summary: Chris Koerner argues that a low-effort way to build a product business is to take a proven product and change its form factor (e.g. gummy vs pill, caffeine in gum). He demonstrates how to use Higgsfield (AI image/video platform, with Nano Banana Pro and Kling 2.5 Turbo) to produce realistic ad creative before building the product, so demand can be tested with Facebook/Instagram ads. He pitches several product ideas: a feminine/colourful rucking vest, nose filters repackaged for cyclists, and niche-targeted creatine gummies. Key takeaway: validate before investing by generating AI ad creative, and reverse-engineer winning Amazon products using Jungle Scout, then niche them down. The video is partly a sponsored/affiliate demo of Higgsfield.

video.title: Forget Dropshipping. Be The Middleman For $800+/Job (Drop-Servicing)

summary: Chris Koerner tours a concrete-leveling (polyurethane foam lifting) operation in Houston with Jeff, a W-2 employee and father who started 90 days earlier and subcontracts all the physical work. Jeff claims almost $20k revenue, 30-40% gross margins and a $2,500 average job. He gets leads via Facebook ads, Nextdoor, Google, referrals, a Replit-built site with chatbots and HighLevel texting, and quotes jobs remotely from photos. Koerner shows the maths that about 36 leads a month and about 5 quoting hours a week could yield $10k/month profit. Key takeaway: a drop-servicing model, where you sell, quote and coordinate while insured subcontractors do the work, can run part-time, though the claims are early-stage and self-reported.

ideas.name: Concrete leveling drop-servicing (subcontracted foam lifting)
ideas.one_liner: Sell and quote concrete leveling jobs to homeowners and commercial owners, subcontract the work to trailer-owning operators and keep a 30-40% margin.

pricing.model: Quote per job based on estimated foam volume; minimum project around $1,000

price_points.label: minimum small job quote when subbing
cost of subcontractor on a small job

pricing.notes: Avoids bidding wars; because he subs out he is more expensive than owner-operators and may close fewer jobs. Conservative foam estimates are built into quotes. Travel time must be factored in (first job at an hour outside town earned no margin).

ideas.delivery: Insured subcontractors with their own foam-lifting trailers do the work. Jeff quotes remotely from photos and phone calls, books jobs never in the same week, takes a 50% deposit, and requires subs to send photos and check-ins. A power washer subbed out 2-3 days later is baked into the quote and upsold for backyards at $100.

30-40% gross margin per job

Own-equipment entry about $120k for a 20ft trailer, or $60-70k for a van
Ongoing costs under about $500-600/month

ideas.time_to_first_revenue: First job sold June 2025, about 2 hours after launching the Facebook campaign; roughly 90 days to almost $20k revenue.

acquisition.how: Paid Facebook ads, SEO, a landing page and chatbots can run with agents. Nextdoor organic and the outbound texting are weaker and PECR-restricted in the UK.

delivery.how: Physical foam lifting by subcontractors. Dispatch, scheduling and photo check-ins can be tooled, but a human must find, vet and manage subs and estimate foam volumes.

billing.how: 50% deposit and balance on completion can be invoiced and chased by software with light approval.

support.how: Chatbots and automated texts handle inquiries and updates; disputes and on-site problems need a human.

uk_applicability.notes: The model of selling and subcontracting a trade works anywhere, but UK concrete is mostly poured on lower-volume sites and has less slab settling than Texas. Foam lifting exists in the UK, but the market is smaller, and PECR limits outbound texting. A UK version would need subcontractors with public liability insurance and a different demand profile.

summary: Chris Koerner explains how to sell database reactivation as a service to small businesses using GoHighLevel templates. He proposes a no-brainer, performance-based offer (10% of revenue generated from emailing/texting a client's past-customer list), walks through importing contacts, triggering a workflow, auto-replies, and A/B testing offers. He then suggests upselling other services (AI voice agents, missed-call text back, review automation, chatbots). The video is promotional for GoHighLevel via his affiliate link, and the revenue maths is hypothetical.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Spencer (Lonear Trash, Texas), a software founder who started a residential trash subscription business by pre-selling 3-month service to ~150-200 neighbours on Facebook after the incumbent hauler degraded. He bought a used under-CDL side-loader truck 100% financed, sourced used bins, and grew via referrals (free month per referral), Facebook ads (CAC $35-100), and branded bins. Claimed ~$50-60k/month revenue, ~$300k first-year revenue and ~40% margin on rough maths, with very low churn. They also discuss municipal truck auctions as a flip or list-selling side hustle, city contracts, and starting cheaper with bulk junk pickup.

video.title: He Tried an Idea From My Video and Made $46k in One Month

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Hunter (Rogersville, near Springfield, Missouri), who started a parking-lot line striping and seal coating business after hearing an earlier Koerner Office episode with Sinko. In his first two months he claims about $22.9k then $46.8k in revenue (just under $50k total), roughly $20k net profit, on about $3k startup cost. Customers came mainly from a single cold email to about 300 Springfield churches (claimed 7-12% response), followed by in-person quotes. Key lessons: offer both striping and seal coating, show up in person, hire help early, and buy reliable equipment.

video.title: The Easiest Way to Build a Local Newsletter

summary: Chris Koerner builds a local newsletter live for a random US city (Roswell, New Mexico) on Beehive in about 90 minutes. He launches a Meta lead-ad campaign with an instant form, connects it to Beehive via Zapier, and gets his first subscribers within about 10 minutes at roughly $1.15 per lead. He explains monetisation through CPM sponsorships, Beehive boosts and recommendations, referrals, paid tiers and merch, with the claim that a subscriber is worth about 50 cents a month. The key takeaway is to acquire subscribers first with cheap paid ads, then sell sponsorships to local businesses. Beehive is an affiliate partner, so the content is promotional.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office, based in Dallas-Fort Worth, runs several newsletters on Beehive

ideas.name: Local city newsletter (Roswell Dispatch)
ideas.one_liner: Build a free local email newsletter for a mid-sized town, grow subscribers with Meta lead ads, and monetise via CPM sponsorships and other revenue streams.
ideas.business_model: Sponsorship ads sold on a CPM basis, plus Beehive ad network and boosts (pay per new subscriber), affiliate links, paid subscriptions, print-on-demand merch and events.
ideas.customer: Readers: local residents (e.g. ages 25-45) of a town of about 50k+ people. Paying customers: local businesses that sponsor the newsletter.
ideas.problem: Local residents don't know what is happening in their town. Local businesses lack a cheap, targeted way to reach residents.
ideas.offer: A free weekly (or more frequent) email with local news, events, deals and places to visit, with sponsor ads included.

pricing.model: Sponsor ads priced per CPM (per thousand opens); the subscriber side is free, with optional paid tiers.
pricing.notes: Publishing more often multiplies ad revenue because ads are sold per send, but it increases workload.

acquisition_channels.details: Meta (Facebook/Instagram) lead-gen campaign with an instant form asking for email only. Geo-targeted to Roswell, NM, with 'reach more people likely to respond' ticked, placements left open, and a 16-second talking-head phone video with captions. Started at $100/day for one day, then dropped to about $20/day. Got 8 leads in about 10 minutes at about $1.15 per lead.

quote.text: Eight leads, $9. Okay, first of all, I'm going to pause this ad because it's working, right, guys? Okay, $1.15 per meta lead.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Beehive recommendations (newsletter cross-promotion) and boosts (pay-per-subscriber referral from other newsletters, e.g. an Albuquerque newsletter).
Referral widget in the email with rewards such as a bumper sticker, a coupon or a PDF guide. Keep the lowest threshold at one referral.
Publish editions to the Beehive-hosted website so search engines and ChatGPT can index them.

ideas.delivery: Write a weekly email in Beehive using a template (Community Pulse), using ChatGPT for research and copy, and send it to subscribers. Welcome email and surveys are automated. Sponsor ads are sold manually by phone to subscribers who are business owners.
unit_economics_claims: Each subscriber is worth about $0.50 per month at a $50 CPM with a 50% open rate on 5 sends a week
Subscribers stay about 2 years, so the lifetime value is about $12

video.title: Marcus Lemonis Opens Up: Depression, Regrets, & Losing Millions

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Marcus Lemonis (The Profit, now The Fixer on Fox; Camping World; Bed Bath & Beyond) in New York. Marcus says he lost about $50 million personally investing in businesses on the shows, has funded over 100 small businesses of which fewer than 10 worked out, and now gives no-strings money (e.g. $55k) instead of taking equity. He talks openly about depression, anxiety, work as self-medication, regret about not having children and about doing TV, and his push to try uncomfortable things like anchoring live news. Advice for beginners: pick one thing, take calculated finite risks, start with small side hustles and never bet the house. His next-decade idea is an 'everything home' platform with homes recorded on blockchain via Bed Bath & Beyond and tZERO.

video.title: How to Make $15k/M on FB Marketplace Selling This ONE Item

summary: Chris Koerner re-interviews Alex Nelson, 'the Shelf Dude' from Utah, who makes custom wooden shelving for storage totes and sells it exclusively through Facebook Marketplace. Alex charges about $40 per tote space, spends about $150 in materials on a $1,000 shelf, quit his job in May 2024 and reached about $15k/month net profit. Since then he has added digital plans, an eight-module course and an installer network on a 70/30 split, because shelving brings no repeat customers. video.title: Beginner's Guide to Dividend Investing: Build a Stock Portfolio That Pays You $5,000/Month

summary: A beginner-oriented explainer on building a dividend stock portfolio targeting $5,000/month in passive income. It covers stock categories (blue chip, dividend growers, high yield, growth), valuation metrics, staggering payout months, contribution milestones assuming 7% total return and 3% yield, and the 4% rule. Key takeaway: it needs roughly $1.2M-$2M invested and decades of consistent reinvestment, so start small and avoid chasing high yields. The speaker promotes a Blossom portfolio and a Webull transfer bonus.

tactics.name: Four-bucket dividend portfolio mix

Hold dividend growers (e.g. Home Depot, PepsiCo) at about 30%
Cap high yield stocks (e.g. Realty Income, Verizon) at no more than 20%
Optionally add growth stocks that pay small dividends (Apple, Microsoft, Visa)
Diversify across sectors such as consumer goods, technology and real estate

Consistent small contributions plus full reinvestment drive compounding; the time horizon matters more than the starting amount.

lessons.lesson: Raise contributions whenever income rises; small increments compound into meaningfully higher passive income.
Diversify across sectors and payout calendars to smooth income and limit single-sector shocks.

Treat the speaker's projections as illustrative: the content mixes yield and total-return assumptions and is US-centric, so UK investors must adjust for ISAs/SIPPs, UK dividend tax and US withholding tax.
This is not a business; it is a passive capital-allocation approach that needs significant capital, so it does not substitute for building an income-producing business.

video.title: How Anybody Can Start This $15k/Month Business

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Tim Mloud ('The Full-Time Flipper'), a former nurse in Muskoka, Ontario, who flips premium used couches bought on Kijiji/Facebook Marketplace in dense city neighbourhoods and resold from five storage units. He did $183k sales and ~$120k gross profit in 2023 working part-time, targeting ~$1,000 profit per couch, with video inspections, keyboard-shortcut scripts and deadline-driven sourcing. He also does $100 dump runs and sells a course. Key takeaway: position yourself to be first when sellers hit deadlines, relocate rather than rehab, and focus on high-value items.

It explains term vs permanent (whole, universal, indexed universal) life insurance, cash value, conversion, dividends and accelerated death benefits, and who each insurer suits. It contains no business idea; it is consumer finance content with quote-comparison links in the description. Takeaway: term gives the most cover per dollar; permanent adds savings at higher cost.

video.title: We Turned Random Words Into $20K/Month Businesses Ideas

summary: Chris Koerner and guest Sam Thompson use a random word generator to brainstorm business ideas live (Office chess set, blue-collar stoicism community, nightclub marketing agency, airport lounge app), and Claude grades the last two. They argue that $500-$1,000/month-per-customer or high-ticket local service businesses (e.g. garage cleanouts at $700) reach $20K/month far more easily than $10-$40/month subscriptions or ecom. They also pitch local newsletters as an audience asset and an agent that buys available city+service domain names. Key takeaway: pick high-ticket offers, start building an asset or audience, and keep working on what works rather than chasing shiny objects.

summary: Chris Koerner tests bolt.new V2 (now integrating Claude Code) by building a PR outreach app live in about an hour with 15-20 prompts. video.title: We Copied His $10K+/Month Business From Scratch in a New City

summary: Chris Koerner and Kyler (22, Utah) replicate Kyler's Facebook Marketplace washer/dryer rental business from scratch in Dallas-Fort Worth, a market saturated after their earlier viral video. They skip name, LLC and website, post a $60/month listing, boost it for $20, buy a cheap set at a garage sale for $125, and deliver and install. In one afternoon they rent two sets for $70/month recurring in about 4 hours of work. They argue competition grows the market, a $20 boost can acquire a customer worth around $1,300, and the bottleneck is the owner's time. Revenue extrapolations are hypothetical and promotional (Koerner sells a membership).

video.title: Make $20K/Month Selling to Clients Who Don’t Flinch at Price

summary: Chris Koerner and regular guest Sam discuss one-person businesses that can reach $20K/month profit without employees. Sam describes testing an AI-written divorce book ($29 ebook, $17 bump, $300 back-end) sold via Facebook ads at roughly break-even CAC, then printing 300 physical copies until Facebook restricted the ads as 'personal hardship' targeting. Chris adds the idea of monetising the book buyers by referring them to divorce lawyers for pay-per-lead or consulting/referral fees, and extends it to niche legal books (DUI, car accident, etc.). The key takeaway is to test quickly rather than over-research, start with the simple pay-per-lead model, and that $20K/month solo is far easier than scaling to a million-dollar team business.

speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office

speakers.description: Recurring guest, runs the Grow Faster community, ecommerce/ads operator; tested the divorce book funnel

pricing.notes: AOV around $42 with bump; about 70% of buyers took the bump per Sam

acquisition_channels.details: Facebook/Meta ads, broad targeting, automatic placements, optimised for purchases using a pixel on the thank-you page; about $100/day; first week $500-700 spend. Ads later blocked from purchase optimisation as 'personal hardship' targeting.

Low-quality AI-written content (V1 was 'AI slop')
Break-even CAC leaves no margin without upsells or lead resale

Giving legal-adjacent advice

acquisition.how: Ad funnel automated; lawyer partnership sourcing via cold email to firms (limited companies, PECR-allowed) is possible but relationship building needs a human.

onboarding.how: Agreeing terms and getting lawyers to share data needs human negotiation.

delivery.how: Lead routing by software is straightforward once buyers are opted in.

video.title: You Can Now Build Apps for Free With Google AI Studio (w/ Google Insider)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Logan Kilpatrick, who leads the developer product team for Google AI Studio and the Gemini API at Google DeepMind. They discuss how vibe coding in AI Studio makes it nearly free to build and ship many small AI apps, and they live-build two apps: a video analysis engine and a voice AI lead-gen agent. Ideas covered include niche single-purpose AI apps, bundles of AI tools for one persona, an AI implementation agency for small businesses, voice AI agents and a text-based AI travel companion. Key takeaway: the cost of building software is now trivial, so take many niche shots, iterate through about 10 prompts, and use vibe-coded demos as outreach. Chris states this is not sponsored but he is a Google shareholder.

video.title: Make $1K an Hour With This Simple Side Hustle

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Wesley, owner of a Grounds Guys franchise in Keller, Texas (DFW), about adding a Christmas lights installation line to a lawn business. They cover pricing by linear foot, a leasing model where the operator keeps and stores the lights, rising margins in repeat years, labour and time per job, insurance, marketing (door hangers, Facebook, yard signs) and low startup costs. Wesley claims one Grounds Guys owner does $1.25M in Christmas lights alone. Key takeaway: recurring, route-dense, leased holiday lighting can have high repeat-year margins, but it is physical, risky work that agents cannot do.

ideas.one_liner: Install, store and remove custom-fit Christmas lights on homes each year, leasing the lights to customers and earning higher margins on repeat years.
ideas.business_model: Annual per-job install fee priced per linear foot; lights leased and owned by the operator; yearly recurring with 10% discounts in years 2 and 3.
ideas.customer: Homeowners in larger homes (example 3-4,000 sq ft house) wanting roofline lights without doing it themselves.
ideas.problem: Hanging lights is risky, time-consuming and fiddly; homeowners must store and fix lights and replace bulbs.
ideas.offer: Professional measured, custom-cut roofline lighting, timer included, installed, serviced if bulbs fail, taken down and stored by the company.

pricing.notes: Permanent lighting is 2-3x the price. Customer-owned lights model priced differently. No extra charge for colour changes (Wesley says they could charge).

Employees do installs.

ideas.startup_cost: $400-500 minimum for materials plus safety gear/ladders; $2-3k typical first year; Wesley spent $4.5-5k on material for about 15 homes.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Same season; marketing starts July, installs in Oct-Nov (supply ships around September).

onboarding.how: Quotes need physical measuring of the roofline on site (could be approximated with satellite imagery tools, not stated).

video.title: 9 Beginner-Friendly Ways to Make $10K

summary: Chris Koerner and his business partner Brandon brainstorm ideas to make $10k in a year, month, week or day. Ideas include vibe-coded apps for die-hard hobby communities (board games, quilting, gardening), Chris's NEFL screener for founder-led network-effect stocks, local AI bootcamps with high-ticket upsells (Brandon has 27 sign-ups), shipping-container storage, luxury garage sales, buying estate-sale leftovers, and pop-up headshot booths. Chris also shows Backyard Fun House, a sport-court business that subs out every trade and gets leads from selfie-video Meta ads at $23-36 each, which he expects to turn $2,500 of ad spend into $25-45k net profit. Key takeaway: cheap AI-built apps and lead ads let you test ideas fast, and you should track ads through to closed deals.

After many door-to-door rejections he mows a lawn for $20 (tipped to $30), then sells $1 water outside a fair using price anchoring to reach $38. He also spots a brokerage-style opportunity: listing a rural man's old tractor and smoker online for a cut. video.title: I Asked AI to Help Me Beat the Stock Market

summary: Chris Koerner shows how he vibe-coded a stock portfolio backtesting app in Replit (Agent 3) to test his thesis that founder-led S&P 500 companies with strong network effects beat the market. He used ChatGPT deep research to find candidates, then built a live Google Sheet using the GOOGLEFINANCE formula, and used GPT for Sheets to score every S&P 500 company 1-10 on network effects and founder leadership for about $15 in credits. Replit then turned the sheet into a filterable dashboard. On his 8-10/8-10 filter over 10 years he reports 22.4% vs the S&P's 9% weighted and 12% unweighted. He shares about a dozen ChatGPT prompts for generating stock-picking theses and says he put the free tool ("Nel Stocks") behind an email form on a domain he bought. The business angle is small: a free, email-gated vibe-coded tool used as a lead magnet. Most of the video is personal investing, not a business.

He explains how he develops tools for his own use, validates demand before building, and grows products through SEO, social content, partnerships, directories, and cross-selling. The key takeaway is to find a real problem, test whether the right customers will pay, and automate recurring work gradually while keeping useful human checks.

tactics.name: Build from a problem you experience yourself
steps: Notice a repetitive or frustrating task in your own work.
Build the smallest tool that solves it for you.
Use it yourself long enough to learn its weaknesses before offering it to others.

quote.text: The best ideas are the ideas that scratch your own itch. So, basically, you're doing a job and then you have a problem at the job
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Validate search demand before building
steps: Use Google autocomplete to find how people complete a query such as “website builder for”.
List roughly 50 to 60 candidate ideas in a spreadsheet.
Check keyword volume and competition, then compare related phrases for the same audience.
Use the results to decide whether a niche has enough demand and a reachable audience.

quote.text: I usually play with it for an hour. I make a list in the Excel for like 50 or 60 ideas and then I bring them back into the keyword research tool
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Try to disprove the idea
steps: Look for evidence that the idea should not be built.
Check whether search demand comes from the intended buyers.
Test one idea at a time and stop spending build time when the evidence is weak.

quote.text: So basically when I build something I'm trying to convince myself that I shouldn't build it
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Use a waitlist as an early demand test
steps: Build a simple landing page with a clear description and a name-and-email sign-up.
Show it to people in the target audience and track sign-ups.
Use the waitlist to learn whether people will take a small step toward the product, not as proof that they will buy.

tactics.name: Ask for pre-orders to check willingness to pay
steps: Offer a pre-booking at a discount before building the full product.
Track how many waitlist users pay, not just how many sign up.
Ask users who decline whether the issue is price, recurring billing, or the audience being wrong.

video.title: $1K a Day From This Simple Side Hustle (Here’s How to Copy It)

summary: Chris Koerner visits Clayton and Haley Bowman, a couple in Cameron, Missouri who run a family pizza tent in a hardware store parking lot, selling pizzas for $15-20. They say 20 orders is $600-700 in a day, with about 20% food cost and 15% other costs for roughly 60% profit, and some nights exceed $1,000; they pay for the spot with occasional lunches. Their advice is to start local and buy used equipment rather than waiting for everything new. Chris then cites other pizza operators (a UK trailer, a California professor at farmers markets claiming $175k net) and demonstrates his home dough recipe and Gozney-style oven technique. Key takeaway: a low-cost pop-up pizza business can have high margins but is entirely physical labour.

video.title: The Most Hands-Off Side Hustle Anyone Can Copy

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Peter Askew (askew.org, Deep South Ventures), who has spent 20 years building small online businesses around exact-match domains, mostly bought patiently at expired-domain auctions. He started by buying neglected but well-ranked mom-and-pop websites and adding AdSense (Travel Envoy cost $10k, earned $1-2k/month and paid back in six months), then bought DudeRanch.com for about $18k and turned it into a flat-fee advertising directory (about 60 advertisers, a little over $50k a year from about an hour a month). He also runs RanchWork, a hand-curated ranch job board ($99+ per posting, 1.3M visits a year), and Vidalia onions sold direct to consumers with a partner farm (100,000 lb shipped this year, using Shopify and ShipStation). Key lessons: let a great domain's type-in traffic and authority be the marketing channel, keep your day job until side projects out-earn it, give partners no-risk offers, and be patient.

tactics.name: Buy under-monetised ranking websites
steps: Google high-CPC terms (e.g. tourism destinations)
Find dated sites ranking top 3 with no ads
Ask owners for analytics
Estimate AdSense income at 1-3% CTR x CPC x 70%
Offer roughly a 6-9 month payback price (e.g. $10k)
Secure the domain first, then migrate content and add ads/affiliates

quote.text: I got to get control of this domain because if I control the domain, I control the whole site
quote.speaker: Peter Askew

tactics.name: Validate an expired domain before bidding
steps: Check search volume for the term and intent (e.g. 'dude ranch vacation' vs band album)
Check state/long-tail variants
Estimate customer ticket size and their margin
Check domain age and GoDaddy traffic stats for type-in traffic
Bid patiently; wait for the right name rather than building ideas first

quote.text: I wanted search volume. I want to fish where the fish are
quote.speaker: Peter Askew

tactics.name: Corner a niche by partnering with the competitor
steps: Notice advertisers cancel one directory but keep the other
Partner with the competing directory
Cancelling both would cost them ~50% of traffic, reducing churn
Eventually buy the partner out

quote.text: if they cancel both of us, they're going to lose about 50% of their traffic
quote.speaker: Peter Askew

tactics.name: No-risk partner offers
steps: Offer to do all the online work for free
Domain owner keeps the domain and points nameservers to you (RanchWork 75/25 split)
Farm keeps fulfilment; you only get paid if you generate sales
Keep talking to people until you find the one who 'just gets it'

video.title: Comfort Is the Trap Keeping You Average. Here’s How to Break Out

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Ben Wilson, host of the history podcast How to Take Over the World, about traits Wilson sees in exceptional leaders and creators. They discuss communication, vision, confidence, action, resilience, focus, timing, and finding work that gives you energy. Examples range from the Wright brothers and Rockefeller to Steve Jobs, Tesla, and small local businesses. The interview offers principles and anecdotes rather than a detailed, proven operating model for a business that AI agents could run.

video.title: The Most Copy-Pastable Online Business (Thanks to AI)

summary: Chris Koerner interviews a Dubai-based builder (name not stated in the transcript) who uses AI coding tools (Cursor, Claude Code) to build programmatic-SEO directory sites. His recipe site Guilty Chef ranks for restaurant-inspired recipes and reportedly gets about 11,000 organic visits a month and about $700-800 a month. His Best Dubai directory ranks near Tripadvisor for restaurant review searches. He demos a scaffold from his own product, 5 Day Sprint, building a protein snacks directory page live, and shows how to duplicate a project to launch more niche sites. The key takeaway is that AI makes niche directory sites cheap to build and clone, but SEO needs patience and the revenue shown is small.

video.title: Can’t Code? The Best Way to Start Making Money Online

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Rob Walling (founder of Drip, MicroConf, TinySeed) about his 'stair-step' method: start with simple step-one businesses such as freelancing, productized services or single-feature add-ons sold in app marketplaces (Shopify, Zoom, Chrome, WordPress, HubSpot; a list of ~75), get to about $10k/month to buy out your day job, then build bigger SaaS. Examples include Castos's founder building a $30k/month podcast-editing productized service, then a seven-figure SaaS, and a developer who bought and revamped three WordPress plugins to $20k/month. Rob explains what is vibe-codable, his 2/20/200-hour validation framework, why pricing at $750-1,000+/month unlocks more marketing channels, vertical vs horizontal vs 'orthogonal' (role-based) SaaS, zoom-in pivots, and choosing customer pain or competitor pain. Chris recounts scraping every US iPhone repair store to build a wholesale parts business doing $150k by month three.

video.title: Watch This Overlooked AI Tool Build Me a Business in 23 Minutes

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates finding, validating and launching a business idea in one sitting using Replit Agent 3. He uses Google Trends and Google autocomplete to spot demand for free invoicing software for contractors, then vibe-codes an AI chat/email invoicing app with Stripe payment links and Resend email, and publishes it on a new domain (invoicefree.com). The app works after fixing email-domain verification, though emails land in spam. Key takeaway: search trends plus autocomplete are a cheap demand signal, and AI app builders can produce a working MVP in under an hour; Koerner says he does not plan to turn it into a business.

speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; builds the app live with Replit Agent 3

ideas.name: Invoice Freely: AI chat/email invoicing for contractors
ideas.one_liner: Free natural-language invoicing app where contractors text, email or chat a request and the customer gets an invoice with a Stripe payment link; revenue from a markup on card processing.
ideas.business_model: Free software monetised by a markup on Stripe card processing (about 0.5% on top of Stripe's 2.9%).
ideas.customer: Small businesses and contractors (tree trimmers, roofers, general contractors, home service businesses, gutter cleaners) who dislike filling in CRM/invoicing forms.
ideas.problem: Invoicing software is painful and rarely industry-specific; contractors on a job site do not want to log into a CRM and fill in name, phone, email and address.
ideas.offer: Free invoicing software where the user types or emails something like 'send an invoice for $800 to Mary Smith for tree trimming services'; the app extracts the details with OpenAI, asks for confirmation, and emails the customer an invoice with a Stripe checkout link. Includes a dashboard of invoices sent, paid and pending.

pricing.model: Free to users; platform earns a processing markup (e.g. 3.4% charged vs Stripe's ~2.9%); users can mark it up or pass it on
pricing.notes: The transcript garbles the figure ('3 12%'); read as roughly 3.4%, i.e. about half a percent on top of Stripe. Not a stated price to customers.

acquisition_channels.details: Host plans a lead capture / email capture / lead magnet on the site and exposure from this video; no real acquisition plan stated.

quote.text: I better get some sort of a lead capture, email capture, lead magnet on this because once this video goes live
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: The YouTube audience is expected to try the app after the video goes live.

ideas.delivery: Software delivered as a web app on a custom domain, built with Replit Agent 3. Uses OpenAI API for natural language parsing, Stripe for payment links and Resend for transactional email. Text/SMS via Twilio was left out of the MVP because of US A2P registration (about 2 weeks).
unit_economics_claims: Even 100 customers could be $1,000/month with almost no cost (hypothetical)
Domain cost $11
Twilio number would cost $1/month
Over 33 million small businesses need invoicing software
ideas.startup_cost: About $11 for the domain plus Replit subscription and API usage (not stated); Resend free plan expected to suffice.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: not stated; a working MVP was built in under an hour, but no revenue and no stated plan to run it as a business

acquisition.how: No acquisition plan exists yet. Inbound routes (SEO, directories, app listings, ads) could be run by agents; cold outreach to sole traders would be restricted in the UK under PECR.

onboarding.how: Self-serve signup and chat interface; an agent can handle setup, with occasional human review.

delivery.how: The product is software: OpenAI parses the request, Stripe and Resend handle payment and email. Deliverability issues (spam folder) need occasional fixes.

billing.how: Stripe processes payments and the platform markup is automatic; the host would handle payouts, tax and Stripe Connect setup.

support.how: AI support agents can field most questions, but payment disputes and failed emails need human escalation.

uk_applicability.notes: Software idea works in the UK with changes: Stripe supported, UK contractors and sole traders need invoices and VAT handling (Making Tax Digital), and a 0.5% markup needs Stripe Connect/payments compliance. A2P registration is US-specific; UK SMS is simpler. Market is very crowded (Xero, FreeAgent, QuickBooks, Zoho).

Invoice emails from a no-reply address landed in spam
Payments markup may need Stripe Connect and regulatory compliance
Early AI-generated app had bugs (wrong $150 amount, emails not arriving)

Host himself says he does not plan to run it as a business

summary: Chris Koerner hosts liquidation expert Shannon, who screens liquidation and government auction sites (Costco/Target liquidation auctions, GovDeals, GSA Auctions) and walks through example lots: plumbing fixtures, train sets, pool floats, furniture, patio furniture, Tesla superchargers, a Blackhawk simulator, electric buses, aircraft and lighthouses. The core playbook is to buy boring, seasonal goods, work backwards from a verified resale price, test demand on Facebook Marketplace before bidding, and scale from pallets to truckloads. Member success stories (pressure washers, patio furniture) are cited as proof. Shannon sells a mastermind and Chris sells a community, so evidence is mostly second-hand and promotional.

summary: Ryan Bartlett describes how he built True Classic from a small initial investment into a large apparel business, focusing on fit, value, comfort, product testing, and paid advertising. He explains how retention, free gifts, customer research, creative, and wholesale helped the company grow, while describing the risks of ad dependence, inventory, and retail attribution. The conversation also covers service businesses such as CRO and email marketing agencies, plus other ideas ranging from dropshipping to small-run apparel fulfillment. The central lesson is to solve a real customer problem, test cheaply, and keep improving what already works.

ideas.name: True Classic men's apparel
ideas.one_liner: Sell comfortable, affordable men's apparel with a fit that makes customers feel more confident.
ideas.business_model: Direct-to-consumer product sales, with additional wholesale and retail distribution.
ideas.customer: Men looking for well-fitting, comfortable apparel at prices below premium brands.
ideas.problem: Bartlett saw men's clothing as poorly fitted, uncomfortable, or overpriced; customers also wanted products that made them look better.
ideas.offer: A plain men's T-shirt designed to fit closely at the shoulders and arms, followed by related apparel including denim, activewear, underwear, joggers, long sleeves, and other categories.

pricing.notes: Standard product prices are not stated. The thresholds and gift offers may vary; the speaker says 'or whatever it is' for the final tier.

acquisition_channels.details: Started with Facebook ads, initially using static creative; later used comedic video ads and scaled spend when results supported it.

quote.text: I was, you know, I should go back and really look at the early days on Meta, but I do remember starting out at 100 a day.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

ideas.delivery: Apparel is made by manufacturers and fulfilled through third-party logistics providers. The company began with one T-shirt in six colors and sizes small through 2XL, then expanded products and sizes. It also sells through wholesale and retail partners.
unit_economics_claims: Bartlett said first-customer acquisition was often around break-even, with profitability depending on retention and repeat purchases.
He said Facebook ROAS above 2:1 made his days look very profitable, while break-even ROAS was around 1.6.
He said the company spent about $60–70 million a year on Facebook ads in recent years.
He said negotiating saved the company tens of millions of dollars a year in fees and product costs.
ideas.startup_cost: Bartlett said the initial $3,000 went mainly to Facebook ads and product development; he negotiated credit terms with a manufacturer to avoid paying for initial inventory upfront.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Sales began slowly; Bartlett recalled an $800 sales day in the first week and said sales were coming within a couple of weeks.

acquisition.how: Ad platforms can handle targeting and delivery, but creative strategy, product claims, and channel decisions need human review.

onboarding.how: Checkout, order confirmation, and lifecycle email flows can be automated; sizing and product questions still need human support.

delivery.how: Software can route orders to a 3PL, but manufacturing, packing, shipping, and returns depend on physical operations.

billing.how: E-commerce checkout and payment collection can run automatically, with people handling exceptions and refunds.

support.how: Automated order updates and help content can handle routine queries; fit, quality, and delivery issues need human escalation.

uk_applicability.notes: The apparel and direct-to-consumer model can work in the UK. The company would need UK-specific sizing, pricing, tax, consumer-rights, returns, and fulfilment arrangements.

risks: Bartlett described the company as close to break-even on first-customer acquisition, so repeat purchases and retention matter.
Heavy dependence on Facebook ads made the business vulnerable to platform and attribution changes.
Apparel requires inventory bets, and retail stores can appear unprofitable when their influence on later online purchases is not attributed.
The guest said 3PL software errors caused split shipments and duplicated shipping costs.
Expanding into new product categories without the same product quality and problem-solving focus can weaken the brand.

tactics.name: Validate demand before committing to a product
steps: Read marketplace reviews to find repeated customer complaints and requests.
Compare competitors' product, price, customer service, and marketing.
Use a small test or dropshipped product to learn whether customers respond before making a large inventory bet.
Treat customer feedback as product input rather than relying only on industry trend reports.

quote.text: go validate please on Amazon and come back to me with something really tangible and then I'll feel much better about investing into product.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Narrow down dropshipping tests
steps: Test a range of products.
Identify repeated winners, such as the fidget spinner Bartlett described.
Build a focused website around a winning product rather than continuing to sell an unfocused mix.

quote.text: Test everything, find your winners, scale the winners.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Solve one clear apparel problem
steps: Choose a specific customer and product problem.
For True Classic, focus on fit, price, and comfort.
Make the product itself demonstrate the benefit, such as showing how the fit changes the wearer's appearance.

quote.text: Once I like figured out the three value props that we kind of live and die by which is like just fit, price and comfort.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Iterate around a winning product
steps: Keep improving the product customers already buy.
Test variations such as curved hems, different fits, and inclusive sizes.
Delay unrelated product categories until the core product and its variations are strong.

quote.text: lean into what works and then do all your iterations against that winner.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Use gift with purchase to introduce adjacent products
steps: Choose a high-quality product from a related category, such as activewear or underwear.
Add it as a gift during checkout and use order thresholds for shipping or additional gifts.
Measure average order value and whether recipients later buy from the new category.
Do not use unwanted overstock as the gift if it will disappoint customers.

quote.text: I did it specifically. Well, number one, boost AOV. That's like the obvious thing, right? Like average order value.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Scale ads with a clear performance rule
steps: Start with a manageable ad budget and increase it when results support the increase.
Bartlett described going from $100 per day to $300 per day within about a week to a week and a half.
If performance collapses, pull spend back rather than continuing blindly.
Compare platform-attributed returns with the full profit and loss statement.

quote.text: Now if I push and I look tomorrow and rorowaz is like 0.2 two I'll pull back, right? Like that's how I thought about it.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Build retention before relying on acquisition cash
steps: Set up welcome, abandoned-cart, and post-purchase email flows.
Use post-purchase upsells to introduce related products.
Track whether customers return and buy across categories.
Reinvest cash when the business can afford to do so.

quote.text: So that comes back to like Clavio, email flows, post-purchase upsells, and abandoned cart flows, welcome flows, optimizing the crap out of all of that.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Diversify channels after finding product-market fit
steps: Use the early paid channel to learn, but avoid becoming dependent on it.
Develop wholesale and retail relationships so the business can reach people who distrust online-only brands.
Use retail presence to build credibility as well as immediate sales.

quote.text: diversifying sooner than later is incredibly important to the success of your brand.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Use a 3PL from the start
steps: Outsource physical fulfillment when the founders cannot reliably handle it themselves.
Review 3PL software and order-routing behavior.
Monitor split shipments and shipping charges because errors can erase margins.

quote.text: We knew like there was no way we were going to be able to tell actually ourselves.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Negotiate cash-flow terms with suppliers
steps: Explain the business's potential to manufacturers and ask them to invest through credit terms.
Ask for a defined credit amount and 60- or 90-day terms.
Talk to multiple potential partners because many may decline before one agrees.
Review supplier and software contracts again as volume grows.

quote.text: our ask was, Give me 20,000 in credit, right? Give me terms on that credit. Give me 60 days. Give me 90 days, whatever it is.
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Make comedy ads explain the product
steps: Work with people who can make genuinely funny creative.
Show a clear before-and-after product reveal.
Include the key product benefit and related categories in the script.
Test iterations and keep the elements that improve results.

quote.text: if you really break down that ad, one of the biggest components that you'll notice is that there's this reveal moment
quote.speaker: Ryan Bartlett

tactics.name: Check marketing attribution with post-purchase surveys
steps: Ask customers where they heard about the brand after purchase.
Compare survey responses with platform-reported performance.
If a channel receives no survey credit and is not showing up in sales, consider stopping spend.

quote.text: If it's not showing up in the post-purchase survey, guess what? It's not netting out.

tactics.name: Use a small free project to prove agency value
steps: Find e-commerce owners in a relevant Facebook group.
Offer to review or improve their email flows for free.
Request read-only access and do not send or publish changes without approval.
Document results as case studies before pitching a retainer.

quote.text: Let me mess with your flows. Let me see if I can get your revenue per recipient up.

tactics.name: Sell agencies on attributable impact
steps: Tie the offer to a measurable business result.
Show the client work or data that supports the proposal.
Avoid sending generic decks that list impressions or contacts without explaining the impact.
Use a flat fee when starting if that is easier to explain and deliver.

quote.text: If you can't do that, you're going to be fighting uphill the entire time.

tactics.name: Prioritize impact over busy work
steps: Learn which outcomes matter to the business before choosing projects.
Put roughly 80% of effort toward high-impact work and 20% toward routine work, as Bartlett advised.
Use AI and agents to reduce repetitive tasks so people can focus on higher-impact work.

quote.text: 80% of your energy towards impactful things for the business, 20% to busy work and learn AI, learn a AI agents

video.title: From Nothing to $20k/month with Email Newsletters: Full Tutorial

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Jazz, who runs Winnipeg Digest, a local events/community newsletter (about 35,000 email subscribers plus about 73,000 social followers) started in April 2024. Jazz explains audience growth via Facebook ads, annual exclusive sponsorships priced at about $12,000 per year, survey-based audience data, and a VA plus Claude/ChatGPT content workflow. He is now vertically integrating by selling Christmas light installation to newsletter readers, with plans for permanent lights and a fractional-CMO-for-equity model. The key takeaway is that a local newsletter is a cheap audience asset to build, sponsor sales are the hard part, and the audience can be monetised further through owned businesses.

ideas.name: Local city newsletter with annual exclusive sponsorships (Winnipeg Digest)
ideas.one_liner: A casual, events-focused local email newsletter plus Instagram account monetised by selling annual exclusive sponsor slots to local businesses.
ideas.business_model: Sponsorship/advertising: annual exclusive sponsor packages (one ad per newsletter), one-off ads, and Instagram posts
ideas.customer: Readers: mainly women aged 35-65 and homeowners in Winnipeg; payers: local businesses such as event venues, dentists, HVAC, plumbing and roofing
ideas.problem: Local businesses lack an engaged local advertising channel; residents lack a single positive source of local events and city updates

pricing.notes: Sell annual exclusivity rather than one-off sponsorships. Currency is not stated explicitly and the host speaks in USD. Jazz is in Canada, so CAD is possible.

acquisition_channels.details: About 90% of ad budget on Facebook ads; best ad is a 15-second video with local monument or drone footage and the text 'struggling to find things to do in [city]' plus '50+ events every week'. Spend about $3,000 a month for roughly 2,000 subs a month now, down from 4-5k a month early on.

acquisition_channels.details: Instagram grown to about 73k followers with reels (restaurant reviews), now carousels; Instagram doubles as a sponsor lead source and a cold-outreach credibility tool.
Seasonal referral guides (top 50 things to do this winter, restaurant and hiking guides) drive shares and signups; giveaways and lead magnets being tested.
Sponsor leads come from inbound Instagram feature requests by young marketing coordinators, who then get sold on newsletter ads on a call; also relationships and outreach from the Instagram account.

ideas.delivery: Two VAs (one on events, one on writing) draft with Claude/ChatGPT; Jazz does a final review at night (about 1 hour). Sent via Beehiiv three times a week, 400-2600 words, fifth-grade reading level.
unit_economics_claims: Subscriber acquisition cost about 15 cents CAD early on, about $1.30 now
Subscriber worth about $8-9 a year if every ad slot sells
Newsletter revenue about $144k a year from annual sponsors
Monthly revenue $12-15k
Time about 20 hrs/week now, about 7 hrs without sponsor chasing, up to 15 hrs/week once delegated
Open rate 56-60%, click rate 8-12%

acquisition.how: Facebook ads and Instagram carousels are largely automatable. Sponsor sales still need calls and relationships, which drag this down.

onboarding.how: A subscriber survey in Beehiiv is automated. Sponsor onboarding and ad drafts are manual but template-able.

delivery.how: Agents can draft the content. Events research, editing and final review currently need VAs and a human, though full automation is being explored.

billing.how: Annual invoices could be automated with standard tools. Jazz tracks sponsors in a semi-custom Notion CRM.

support.how: Little support is needed. Sponsor relationship management is mostly human.

uk_applicability.notes: Local newsletters work in UK towns and cities. The Beehiiv survey is fine under GDPR with consent. Use opt-in signups only. Pick a market without an existing local newsletter. The population of 100-150k+ rule of thumb transfers to UK towns and boroughs.

risks: Selling local businesses on newsletter advertising is hard
Sponsors can run out; revenue caps around $500k per year
Subscriber acquisition cost rises as the market saturates
Open rates can drop; aggressive list cleaning can remove real readers
Founder face association makes the asset harder to sell

lessons.lesson: First-mover advantage in an underserved local market lowers acquisition costs and creates a monopoly position.
Exclusivity and annual terms are the product; sell the monopoly over a local audience rather than impressions.
Own audience lets you vertically integrate and capture far more value than third-party ad networks; ad-only monetisation caps out.

A time-compounding business where audience grows with the years is attractive because it is hard to lose.

video.title: Start This Simple Side Hustle Before Everyone Else Does

summary: Chris Koerner ranks five mobile/low-footprint sauna and cold plunge businesses in the US, from Denver Mobile Sauna (5th) to Purely Nomadic Sauna (1st). He pitches the sector as fast-growing, with claimed $10-50k/month operators and around 50% margins. Common themes are Facebook ads or Marketplace for leads, partnering with gyms and studios, tiered pricing, and a free first session. The last third is an interview with Danny of Purely Nomadic Sauna in Michigan, who is only 3-4 months in and has no revenue figures yet. The numbers are mostly second-hand and unverified.

Website bookings; the host implies customers arrive at the site intending to book hourly.

2-3 weekend rentals = extra $1-2k/month

video.title: How to Find the Best Undervalued Deals (For Beginners)

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates how he finds potential off-market RV park acquisitions by scraping Google Maps listings, cleaning and validating phone data, then texting owners and following up by phone. He screens a prospect by asking about occupancy, seasonal pricing, utilities, acreage, and operations, and explains his target of at least a 10% cap rate. A seller describes a seasonal lakeside campground with 80–85% occupancy and different prices for shoreline and inland sites. The video offers a practical sourcing workflow, but the demo does not show a completed acquisition, and several response-rate figures are inconsistent.

ideas.name: Off-market RV park acquisition
ideas.one_liner: Find RV park owners through map listings, contact them directly, and evaluate potential acquisitions against a target cap rate.
ideas.business_model: Buy income-producing RV parks and earn revenue from site rentals. Seller financing is discussed as a possible way to reduce cash required at purchase, not as a guaranteed outcome.
ideas.customer: For deal sourcing, RV park owners who may consider selling. After acquisition, campers and RV owners who rent sites.
ideas.problem: The buyer needs a repeatable way to find and assess parks that are not listed for sale. The sellers' specific problems are not stated.
ideas.offer: Approach park owners directly, learn about the property's occupancy and operations, and consider an offer based on net operating income and other value levers. Koerner says he targets at least a 10% cap rate.

pricing.model: Acquisition price based on property income and a target cap rate; ongoing income from rented sites.

price_points.unit: annual net profit in illustrative example
price_points.label: Example income used to discuss valuation

price_points.unit: purchase price ceiling in illustrative example
price_points.label: Koerner says he would try to pay under this amount for the example

pricing.notes: The $100,000 income and under-$1 million purchase price are an illustrative calculation, not a reported transaction.

acquisition_channels.details: Uses Outscraper's Google Maps data scraper to find RV parks by category and state, then reviews listing fields such as phone type, owner verification, ratings, and photos.

quote.text: So this is outscraper and I want to show you how I use outs scraper but then I didn't want to have to wait for it to scrape.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Filters for cell numbers, adds a city name as a personalized variable, and sends a short first text to start a conversation. He follows up with people who respond. In the UK, unsolicited marketing texts to individuals and sole traders require consent under PECR.

quote.text: The best results come when you're willing to play the long game and just seek to start a conversation on the first message as opposed to ask them right up front if they're interested in selling.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Calls a seller who asks to speak by phone; Koerner says he researches the property before calling. This is a response to the seller, not a cold call.

quote.text: Give me a call. I don't do business over text message. Okay, I will. I like to do a little more research before I call them so I don't sound like an idiot.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: The video focuses on finding and assessing acquisition targets. After purchase, the owner would operate the park and rent sites; the transcript does not explain Koerner's post-purchase staffing, maintenance, or guest-service process. The seller in the example says he manages his park seasonally.
unit_economics_claims: Koerner says he targets a minimum 10% cap rate.
He illustrates that $100,000 in annual net profit would imply trying to pay under $1 million.
A capped Outscraper search in the demo is quoted at $10; this is lead-list cost, not a full business startup cost.
He says 129 scraped listings yielded 129 cell phones from a 500-listing search, or 26%.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The demonstrated scrape is quoted at $10 for a search capped at 500 listings; this is not a complete startup-cost estimate.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated for a purchase or operating revenue. The demonstrated scrape is quoted as taking 7–25 minutes.

acquisition.how: Map scraping and data cleaning can be automated, but the demonstrated unsolicited SMS approach is restricted in the UK for individuals and sole traders without consent. UK cold email to limited companies may be used where appropriate; cold calls must be screened against TPS/CTPS. Seller negotiation remains human.

onboarding.how: Property records, financials, site visits, and purchase documents require human review and negotiation; no automated onboarding process is described.

delivery.how: Operating an RV park involves physical property, utilities, and guest needs. The video does not describe automation for that work.

billing.how: No billing system is described. Site rental billing could use software, but setup and exceptions would need human oversight.

support.how: Guest and seller conversations are handled personally in the example; no automated support system is described.

uk_applicability.notes: The property-investment and map-research approach can work in the UK, but the demonstrated US cold-text workflow cannot be copied to UK individuals and sole traders without consent under PECR. UK cold email can be used for limited companies, and cold calls must be screened against TPS/CTPS. Property, planning, and seasonal-demand assumptions also need local assessment.

risks: The transcript presents seller financing as a possibility, not a guaranteed way to buy with no money down.
The example's reply figures do not reconcile: four initial replies from 129 recipients are described as a 10% response rate, and a later count is 23 responses.
The speaker says listing owner names may be missing or inaccurate, data can include the wrong business category, and duplicate phone rows can disrupt data matching.
The demonstrated cold SMS tactic would require a UK-compliant lawful basis and appropriate consent where the recipient is an individual or sole trader.
The demonstration does not establish the seller's asking price, net operating income, required capital works, or whether a deal closes.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Rex Lindsay, owner of Cozy Pros, a Phoenix home-performance business selling attic insulation removal/re-insulation, Aeroseal duct sealing, duct cleaning and air scrubbers, mostly via Facebook ads offering a free attic inspection. Rex says he moved from ~100 in-house employees to subcontracting nearly all installation work, with a project manager on site, citing lower insurance, equipment and quality-risk burden. He gives average ticket (~$10k), margin structure (~52% gross, 15-20% net target), lead cost (~$75) and ad return claims. Key takeaway: learn lead generation and sales, subcontract the labor, and use cheap front-end offers (duct cleaning, free inspection) to upsell large tickets.

summary: Chris Koerner demonstrates how he validates an online business idea before launching, using the example of a cheap, AI-enabled QuickBooks/Xero competitor for businesses with 0-10 employees. He runs the same research prompt through Perplexity Labs, Manus, Claude Opus 4.1 and ChatGPT-5 agent mode, mines Reddit complaints with GummySearch, and explains paid polling with PickFu ($1 per response). The research converges on unreliable bank feeds, rising and unpredictable pricing and poor support as the top pain points, suggesting a 'cheap price forever, never breaks' positioning. He then builds a landing page on Carrd connected to a Namecheap domain and Beehiiv in eight minutes, and announces LazyBooks at $19/month, built for 0-10 employee businesses.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Cody Schneider about AI-powered Etsy print-on-demand: use Everbe to find best-selling Etsy products, generate similar vector graphics with the ChatGPT image API, automate the pipeline with n8n (workflow JSON written by Claude/Perplexity), push to Printify and publish to Etsy for a volume game of thousands of listings. They also cover Google Shopping ads arbitrage, a comparison with dropshipping, other POD/digital product categories, and a pitch to build merch stores for creators on a 5% revenue share via cold email. Key takeaway: AI image generation removes the design bottleneck, but results are unproven and the numbers are speculative.

lessons.lesson: Use data tools to find proven demand rather than guessing, then copy the pattern.
Volume strategies expect a power-law outcome: a small share of listings drive most revenue, so surface area matters.
AI removes the human labour bottleneck in creative production, which was previously the moat.
LLMs can write automation workflow files, making complex tools like n8n usable by non-coders.
Print-on-demand carries no inventory or sunk cost, which makes it a better business model than dropshipping and possible to sell.
Pitch with finished examples, such as a built store, rather than abstract proposals; it makes the offer easy to say yes to.
A first business is mostly for acquiring skills; downside is small and the learning compounds into the next venture.

evidence_quality.rationale: Cody describes a method and past Etsy experience but gives no concrete revenue or results for the AI version; income figures are hypothetical and the creator-merch idea is brainstormed live. Little verification of Etsy policy on mass AI listings.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Chris promotes his TKOwners paid community and newsletter/podcast; Cody has a friend who owns Everbe, which he recommends.

video.title: These Genius Business Ideas Are Hidden All Over America

summary: Chris Koerner and his long-time friend Nick trade 'hidden' state-by-state business ideas: beach weddings as a service, reselling merch from cult regional attractions that don't sell online (the Texas Snacks/Buc-ee's model), rentable movie vehicles and TV-location tours, drive-a-tank experiences, goat grazing for brush clearing, and reselling unclaimed or left-behind items. Chris also announces a 'business in 50 states in 50 days' YouTube series inspired by Ryan Trahan and frames paid shout-outs on big creators as cheap media buying. They close on Meta's earnings and why small home-service businesses wrongly conclude Facebook ads don't work. Key takeaway: look for proven local models (experiences, middleman/brokering, unsold merch) and copy them into other markets, using cheap targeted ads or content for distribution.

video.title: This $15K/Person Grant Feels Like a Cheat Code

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Hector, who built an online, grant-funded trade school in Texas (about $2.4M in year one) and now consults for people starting schools. The core idea is that US workforce grants (WIOA-style, called 'WA' in the transcript) pay $5k-$15k per student, so a school can white-label a course and have the government pay the tuition. Variants include embedding a school in an existing business that struggles to hire (e.g. CNAs), on-the-job-training wage subsidies, and a school plus staffing placement combo. The key takeaway is that the arbitrage is navigating grant bureaucracy and enrolling students, but it is heavily US-state-specific.

speakers.description: Texas-based former online trade school operator, now consultant helping people start grant-funded trade schools

ideas.name: Grant-funded online trade school (white-label courses)
ideas.one_liner: Start an online vocational school, white-label courses, and have state workforce grants pay $5k-$15k per student.
ideas.business_model: Tuition paid by government workforce grant per enrolled student; margin over white-labelled course cost.
ideas.customer: Laid-off workers, people on food stamps/benefits, warehouse, retail and fast-food workers, nonprofit and shelter clients who qualify for the grant.
ideas.problem: People qualify for free training grants but find the process bureaucratic and do not know about it; there is a shortage of tradespeople and technicians.
ideas.offer: Free training (plus free laptop or VR goggles) toward a certificate in a technician or remote-capable field, paid for by the state grant.

pricing.model: Grant pays per student, varying by state, region and field
pricing.notes: White-label course cost $800-$1,000 (later $500 example); equipment such as goggles $200-$300 or a laptop.

acquisition_channels.details: Pitched the grant to churches, church groups, women's shelters, nonprofits, workforce development centres and chambers of commerce as community/referral partners; spent $0 on marketing.

quote.text: I went I spent zero dollars in marketing. I just went knocking on church doors and getting involved with church groups
quote.speaker: Hector

acquisition_channels.details: Got on Twitter, which produced his first consulting call (a flight attendant school in Minnesota).

ideas.delivery: Online courses licensed from a white-label provider, delivered remotely; some students receive laptops or VR goggles. Hands-on trades like welding or phlebotomy need in-person components or employer externships.
unit_economics_claims: Grant pays $5k-$15k per student depending on region, state and field
White-label course costs $800-$1,000, rest is margin
Scaled to about $2.4M in year one on grants in Texas
Average graduate earns $25-$30 an hour
ideas.startup_cost: Low: white-label course about $500-$1,000 plus $200-$300 goggles or a laptop per student; state licensing fees and waits not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Varies by state: easy states quick, tough states wait 6 months to 2 years for approval (Florida, California, New York, Washington).

acquisition.how: Relied on in-person church and community outreach; enrolment is sales-driven. Online ads or SEO could be added but the grant message needs trust-building.

onboarding.how: Grant paperwork, eligibility checks and student enrolment can be partly handled by forms and CRM but require human government liaison.

delivery.how: Pre-built white-label online courses are largely software-delivered; some hybrid hands-on components need humans.

billing.how: Reimbursement from state or workforce boards needs compliance documentation and human follow-up.

support.how: Student support and job placement help can be mostly agent-handled with human escalation.

uk_applicability.notes: Depends on US state/federal workforce grants; the UK has different funded-training systems (e.g. apprenticeship levy, Skills Bootcamps, Adult Education Budget) with approved-provider registers and Ofqual/OFS rules, so the model would need a full rebuild.

risks: State licensing delays (up to two years in some states)
Grant rules vary by region and can change
Hard to get trust from skeptical students ('what's the catch')
Compliance and reimbursement-timing risk
Some trades cannot be taught online

video.title: 8 Best ChatGPT Tools to Make Money With (Ranked)

summary: Chris Koerner ranks eight ChatGPT models/products from worst to best (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, Sora, GPT-4.5, Deep Research, o3/o4-mini, ChatGPT Agent, gpt-oss), explains each and suggests ways to monetise them, then adds GPT-5 as a 'number 0.5'. Cheap models suit commoditised wrapper services (bulk descriptions, captions, chatbots, cold email), while more specialised capabilities (deep research consulting, technical services, agent implementations) command higher prices. His top pick is implementing the open-weight gpt-oss privately on company servers for big setup fees plus monthly maintenance, because data privacy is what stops companies adopting AI. Key takeaway: specialised, measurable-ROI AI implementation beats low-skill wrapper services.

video.title: If We Had to Make $1M Fast, We’d Start These Businesses

summary: Chris Koerner and fellow podcaster Nick trade ideas for reaching a $1M business in six months. They cover RV rentals, 30 AI wrappers in 30 days, offshore AI-native talent placement, AI cost-savings audits for large corporations, rolling up dormant newsletters, a 'hero workflow' AI automation agency (Chris built a GoHighLevel after-hours voice agent for garage door firms and got a yes in 57 minutes), liquidation flipping, buying a business to add AI value, glamping, HVAC coil cleaning, Bingo Loco-style events and a mowing fantasy camp. Final picks: buy a business plus AI, liquidation, RV rentals, and AI automation for small businesses. Key takeaway: pick one high-impact plug-and-play workflow per niche, validate demand with data before buying assets.

summary: Chris Koerner interviews 23-year-old Kyler, who rents used washers and dryers to renters via Facebook Marketplace in Utah, claiming about $10K/month with 120+ sets, no employees and 5-10 hours a week. His 'Post, Rent, Buy' process validates demand with a listing before buying any machines. Used Whirlpool direct-drive sets are sourced free or cheap, and he also covers appliance delivery for used-appliance shops as a side income. summary: Chris Koerner live-validates a business in about 56 minutes: an AI after-hours voice answering service for home service businesses, starting with garage door repair companies in Dallas-Fort Worth. He scrapes Google Maps leads with Outscraper, cleans them in Google Sheets, keeps mobile numbers, bulk-texts 50 owners via Straight Text, then pitches a pay-per-closed-lead offer. He builds a demo voice agent in GoHighLevel in minutes. He gets about a 40-50% response rate and one 'yes' (interested), then extrapolates to a hypothetical $1.2M/yr. Key takeaway: validate demand with outreach before building anything, though the one yes is not a closed sale and the texting method is problematic in the UK.

ideas.name: AI after-hours voice answering for garage door repair companies

ideas.customer: Owners of small local garage door repair companies (high-ticket home service, not private-equity-consolidated) in DFW, extendable across the US.
ideas.problem: Owners do not answer the phone after hours and lose jobs worth hundreds to thousands of dollars; competitors send callers to voicemail.
ideas.offer: A 24/7 AI voice agent that answers, captures name and address, emails a call summary and transcript, and can forward urgent calls to the owner. Free setup, no contract, no upfront money, pay $50 only when a lead closes.

Do you still fix garage doors? I found you on Google Maps'), with a city name as a variable, then sent the pitch only to those who replied.
